We will be happy to help you again. We wish you the best in your staying in Chile, we hope that you can achieve your goals while you're here. Best regards in behalf of City Trekking Guide Team Ignacio!

review_text: What do reading Cosmo, eating Cheetos and drinking Diet Coke have in common with San Pedro de Atacama? All will leave you feeling unsatisfied with a vague feeling of dismay about the human race. This holds true for just about every place we visited inside the town of San Pedro de Atacama from the church to the "handicraft" market. Many people travel to San Pedro de Atacama because it has been developed for tourists and it is located in a spectacular area of the Chilean Andes and Altiplano. This is the type of tourist town we normally avoid and the minute we arrived, we were incredibly grateful that we had booked a vacation lodging 5 miles outside of town. The town is a collection of upscale (for Chile) boutiques, restaurants, tour providers, and hotels. The setting has a definite colonial theme – the streets are unpaved, narrow and mostly one way alleys. Many of the buildings are adobe or adobe and with old beautiful wood doors and gates. Unfortunately, much of the charm has been lost with the overflow of relatively wealthy traveling twenty-somethings from mostly western countries. The downtown square where the church is located seems to have no soul – it reminded us of a town built by Disney, a fantasy constructed only as a tourist destination. Most of the visitors seem to avoid leaving town to see the sights except on tours which are neatly packaged to ensure a full day of “the usual suspects”. The lakes at Miniques, the Valley of the Moon, etc. Visitors seem to consist of two types. The first are local Chileans on vacation to see the sights around the town and a few destinations in the Altiplano. These visitors travel primarily in buses driven by suicidal drivers with no regard for speed limits, parking, or other basic courtesies. Visitors pour out of the buses, often taking over a stop or location, snap some photos and leave within minutes for the next photo opportunity. The second type of visitor and more offensive to our way of thinking are the backpacking toting, college kids with their Iphones/Ipads, guitars, torn jeans, and designer clothes hanging around the Central square until it is time to go back to the hostel or out drinking. Sure, most of these kids are just trying to have a good time, meet new friends and have an adventure, but it must seem particularly offensive to the locals to see westerners pretending poverty while spending thousands of dollars for travel to another country. The income disparity in Chile is real and it is most obvious in towns like San Pedro de Atacama. In that sense, you can see a true picture of Chile here but not in the central part of town or during activities that are set up for tourists. Travel a half-kilometer outside the tourist district to the north and west where many of the locals that work in the tourist facilities live. These “houses” are made out of timber scraps, pallets, corrugated roofing, plastic and scavenged items. Maybe we delude ourselves by claiming to be different. One of the main reasons we typically avoid towns like this is that while they do provide jobs, the jobs they provide are usually not well paying good jobs. They do exploit local labor, overcharge tourists and control what visitors can and can’t see and experience. We try to spend our money in businesses that are actually owned by small local families. We prepare most of our own meals with local products and visit towns that others avoid or miss completely. This is a vacation we find adventurous. It also helps us feel that we are making a small difference with how and where we spend our vacation dollars. The Church of San Pedro de Atacama is one of the least interesting that we visited in Chile. The most interesting part of it is the history which is described inside of the Church. The handicraft market in San Pedro de Atacama is made up primarily of imports from Peru, Bolivia and other nearby countries. You will not find locally made handicrafts here. My recommendation: avoid San Pedro de Atacama. Stay outside of town and visit the smaller towns in the area – many of which are not mentioned the guidebooks. Try Toconao, with its central square and friendly locals, and locally made handicrafts. Or Socaire, with its historic and beautiful stone farming terraces.

review_text: We booked Roberto online while in Easter Island (with lousy internet) and had no requests regarding itinerary except a very open-ended Valparaiso and surrounds. Roberto arrived early to meet us at our airport hotel. His 4x4 car fitted the 4 of us comfortably. We drove to Valparaíso via Viña del Mar with Roberto pointing out things of interest and answering all our questions. We had had three weeks travelling right from top to bottom of Chile and this was our last day so we had lots of questions. Roberto was fabulously knowledgeable about the history and social economy of the country and region. His English was excellent (sophisticated use of words and he 'got' the nuances). We weren't madly impressed with Viña del Mar (too much like home) so spent our time in Valparaíso and skipped the wineries because we loved Valparaíso so much (and despite how fabulous the Chilean wines are, we've seen many wineries before) so this was just what we wanted. Roberto found things and places in Valparaíso that we never would have found by ourselves and even introduced us to artists. What was most fabulous was that Roberto was prepared to be completely flexible and we were able to play it by ear and adapt our day as we found things that were interesting to us. So much fun and truly an experienced local!

review_text: When you come down the hill into Puerto Varas, suddenly the lake just opens up in front of you. In the early morning, there will often be gray clouds and mist obscuring the million dollar view of the volcanoes across the lake. Once those clouds part as if the lake were a stage, you feel as if you could be in the Alps - except for the fact that Lake Llanquihe is enormous! One of the best views of it if you want to take in the whole thing is from Osorno Volcano. Yes, the water is pretty cold but it's clear and hopefully clean. There's a great beachfront in Puerto Varas where there are places to swim, eat, shop and stay. One of the cool options too is to bike along the shores of the lake. There are also tons of places to stay and eat outside of Puerto Varas too. If you're looking for some peace and quiet - those places, no Puerto Varas, would be for you!

review_text: Not being a beer drinker per se, I wanted to see if I could locate a very light beer via a small tasting. To acquire that sample I had to be somewhat of a ‘Con Permiso’ person. The first was not available or so I understood the ‘hand across the throat’ to movement to mean, the second choice I had to wait another 5 minutes, and received a tiny squirt of bubbles into the glass which settled out as 1/2 a soup spoon full, barely enough to taste. I noticed some time later other customers were receiving at least 75cc freely for tasting. I get the 75cc from what they sell as their 150cc glass, the one I was to order later. We ordered a Spaghetti Western pizza and the first 2 choices of beer were not available. The have attempted to help you in the size of the beer you wish to purchase by using Beer Stein symbols of varying size at the top of their beer menu. NOTE.. there is absolutely NO relationship between the size of the Beer Stein symbol and what you receive. My selection was based on the first beer stein , what I received was a small Boarding House juice glass. So small I though it was a large sample. The pizza eventually arrived though I did see 2 tables which arrived and ordered at least 10 minutes after our order was placed, receive their pizzas .. in one case the same Spaghetti Western. They seem not to understand it makes sense to deliver the knifes and Forkes before the food OR at least with the food. While we sat waiting for our utensils the chap at the adjacent table offered us theirs as they were still awaiting their order. The staff this Sunday afternoon were lacking standard operational procedures and / or they were poorly trained. The tables and chairs are the result of wooden Pellets used for transport of heavy material. Nice idea but bloody uncomfortable, especially so when the waiting time is excessive. Nice to locate the place and drive along that section of road but it is not a place I would hurry back to for a pizza.

review_text: We booked 3 tours with MTO via Viator. If you like reliable service I’d recommend steering away from this company. 1. Transfer from Santiago Airport to hotel: I had 3 times confirmed the flight arrival time and meeting location with the company, however when we arrived the driver was nowhere to be seen. We waited, kept looking and tried calling the company (nobody picked up after multiple calls). Eventually we had to find alternative transport to the hotel. Viator was good at refunding our money but nothing worse than arriving late at night to a new country with your transfer not there. 2. Wine tour to Santa Rita winery: Driver showed up 30 min late to our hotel for pick up. Again we tried to contact the company by phone and WhatsApp but no response... the tour itself was great. 3. Transfer from hotel to cruise ship: this was smooth, the driver was there right on time and there were no issues. If you think 1/3 is good, with no responsive customer service then this is a company for you. However if you prefer reliability look elsewhere. Chile is a beautiful country and I’m sure there are better services to book for transfers. Viator should find another partner.

review_text: Cicloaustral organized a wonderful bike trip on the northern CA for our family of four. Claudia and Fernando arranged for us to stay in nice lodges, rustic refugios, or campgrounds, depending on our preferences and what was available in remote locations. If 5-star luxury and rigid schedules are important for you this might not be your trip and this part of Patagonia might not be your happy place. If a little adventure and flexibility are higher priorities, you’ll be in very good hands. We had our own guide Max, who took great care of us, treated us like family, and provided lots of background info about everything from bugs to glaciers, and personal insights about Patagonia’s past and present. The vistas are stunning—every day we’d bike through multiple places that would be worth an entire trip in themselves. We enjoyed the flexibility to follow our own schedule, taking some detours to do a little extra exploring along the way when we had the time and energy. It’s Patagonia, so you might be cruising in warm sunshine one day and slogging through cold rain and wind the next, zipping along a smooth road in a river valley or being jostled by potholes and washboard ruts on the dirt road that climbs and descends through Pumalín NP. We loved the challenges and the friendly people. It was inspiring to bike for 11 days through this magical land. I highly and happily recommend Cicloaustral.

review_text: I booked the full day trip to Peulla from Puerto Varas through GoChile which was a good booking experience although the actual tour operator was Turistour. We were picked up at our hotel on time around 8am by van and transferred to a larger bus in downtown opposite the Turistour office. After visiting the Petrohue waterfalls, along with passengers from several other buses, nothing that special, we were taken to the Lagos Andinos Catamaran for the crossing of Lake Todos Los Santos. In retrospect, as we had two days in Puerto Varas, and it was mid to low season(likely not advisable in high season) I might have booked the trip when in Puerto Varas for the day with the clearest weather. The staff were professional and we got better at zip lining as we proceeded down the nine segments. A meal at the Hotel Peulla was included. This was adequate and the service good. Then it was back to the boat for the trip back getting in around 5.30. A good day out but the weather did co operate for us.

review_text: I had only a short time in Santiago and decided to get some insight to Chilean expression of two of my passions, food and wine. Jose and Connie were able, at short notice, to accommodate me on a tour of markets and cooking workshop (one day - this review) and tour of Casablanca wineries (second day - also reviewed on Trip Advisor). On both occasions, there was one other couple plus myself. We met Connie at the Central Market (fish - and one of top 5 in world according to Nat Geo) and spent a couple of hours touring it and associated markets nearby - fruit & vegetable, flower, meat, you-name-it (collectively, way better than Adelaide's central market, for those of you that know it). Connie was extremely knowledgeable about Chilean food culture and ingredients - and focussed on every day food that Chileans eat. She also bought ingredients for the hands-on workshop. We then went (short taxi ride) to their kitchen in Bella Vista. She had everything ready for us (including our own aprons - which we kept) for the dishes what we were cooking/making (pisco sour, pebre(salsa), Chilean ceviche, traditional empanadas, pears in read wine with crème anglaise). We all contributed to the cooking - and then eating. Great fun and very tasty. Connie also provided some decent Chilean white and red wines to pair with the dishes. Finished around 5pm - so we got great value! Connie was very friendly, fun and relaxed. I am guessing she could be very flexible around the recipes to be cooked. Highly recommend.

review_text: We have just completed the 4 day tour from San Pedro de Atacama to Uyuni and back again. This was without doubt one of the best natural wonders I have ever seen. But here are some practicalities: 1) World White Travel will want your cash and for you not to pay on card. This might be an issue if you come to SPDA with limited cash as there are only 4 ATMs, of which none were working when we arrived. After some negotiations they agreed to take half as a credit card payment and half as cash. Clearly cash has more benefits for them... 2) Bring plenty of sun cream (don't be fooled by the cool early morning breeze), snacks, water and toilet roll. 3) You probably won't want too much alcohol as the altitude kicks in (particularly day/night 1). However you can buy beers in the villages you stay in. We had 4 or 5 over the couple of days. 4) I'll be honest here - you need a bit of luck, especially in February. First of all, you will be separated into groups of six for each 4 wheel drive. My wife and I had the luck that our car was filled with 4 other amazing people. Although the scenery speaks for itself, you spend 3 full days with these people so its key that you get on. The weather in February is said to be unpredictable in the southwestern part of Bolivia. We were fortunate as we were largely blessed with partly cloudy skies throughout, it did rain heavily overnight on the 2nd night. But it's a risk / reward business and seeing the reflections on the salt flats was dreamlike. Fortunately we also saw a dry section of the flats so we got the best of both worlds. But the wet part was definitely the more incredible. Our driver, Felix, was a legend too. 5) Bring paracetamol- it will help with the altitude. You go nearly as high as 5000m. 6) it's handy to have a Spanish speaker in the car to help translate. Fortunately one of car could speak fluent Spanish so helped to put colour into what you were seeing. 7) The accommodation is fairly basic but what would you expect in the desert. The first night has no shower but the last two do. You will get dorm rooms on night one, rooms of 2 on night 2 and rooms of 2/3 on the last night. 8) the food is fine. A mixture of soup, spag bol, chicken escalope, tuna & sweetcorn and salad was the standard. Breakfast was usually pancakes. 9) don't expect much once you've done the salt flats. The 3rd night is only there as they can't make it back from Uyuni to SPDA in one go. 10) toilet charges are between 1 and 6 Bolivianos. review_text: First our driver was okay on the way to the hot springs unlike his "wild joyride" return at about midnight speeding through small towns and then through the streets of Santiago! I was shocked at the bathroom facilities at the hot springs! There was no electricity, the floors were filthy! There was no way I'd step foot on that floor and luckily even in my 60's thank goodness I could dress relatively easily while balanced on one foot for a short time! (good thing I'm still in decent shape!) IF you do this trip bring water shoes, because of the poorly maintained hot springs both inside the bathroom and outside where the hot springs are! (This apparently is a privately owned establishment that the tour company has an arrangement to go) One of the mid 30's man in my group said when he went to change in the bathroom that he hopes he doesn't get athlete's foot or something else while he goes in there! On the way to the hot springs they stop at a small waterfall, this is not a big deal really since its quite small compared with Many others I saw in Southern Chile just a few days before. Now, the BBQ...while the food was quite good it was not what an American thinks of as a BBQ! There were no plates, you were literally served using fingers to both take off the serving dish as well as eating! (no plates or silverware) Like I said earlier the food is good but IF you are expecting a feast, you will be disappointed, it's more like light appetizers! (dessert was 2-3 bite size cookies) The price per person in my opinion was a bit pricey considering! During my 15 day trip to Chile this was a tour I had really looked forward to doing, but unfortunately was the worst compared to all the other 9 tours we did during our trip. Review of: Santiago: Cajón del Maipo, Hot Springs, Waterfall & Chilean BBQ Hi! First of all I want to clarify that we are not the owners of the Hot Springs, so big part of your review you should leave it to the Hot Springs owners, as Andes Experience we noticed the lack of maintenance on the Hot Springs bathrooms so now we actually own a Lodge (where the BBQ is) where you can find high end bathrooms even with showers if you want to use them, all thinked for your comfort. Related to the waterfall, we can't control how much water flows in it, as you came in late March, you will not find so much water as we are deep into the dry season, but even that, is a really nice place also to see the different landscapes surrounding besides the waterfall. As we offer a Chilean BBQ, the most common BBQ in Chile is "finger food" Style, where you taste some cold appetizers, hot entrances, grilled vegetables and main course that is the Beef, there is food in abundance, the guides will serve you until you say that you are full, same with the drinks, as is an all you can eat and drink Chilean Style BBQ. I personally after your review, checked the cameras installed in each Jeep for safety and saw that the driver was not speeding, as a company we really focus on this safety aspect and we are constantly checking our drivers and supervising through the cameras. I think it just was your sensation on driving in a big jeep in small country side roads. Sincerely, Ignacio Prado Owner.

We then continued on to another beautiful property, the Quintessence Alpaca Ranch to watch baby alpacas romp around in the mountain breeze at the base of the Andes. The owners are using traditional methods to process their yarns and it was great to get the personal tour from the warm and friendly proprietress, Sonya. The peaceful setting and happy alpaca babies put a smile on everyone’s face. Our final stop was a a small vineyard called Flaherty Wines. The owner/chef prepared a lunch that could rival any 5 Star restaurant and was topped off with a tasting of their signature wines. Any one of the 3 stops would have made a fun and unique day, but having all 3 in one day was a perfect day trip to discover the beauty of Chile. Mick is very knowledgeable about the area and the local wine production and is a delightful guide and travel companion. 5 Stars for Mick!! I would highly recommend the Wine Safari and Ride De Vuelta 😄

review_text: The landscape and the tour are incredible, but the details of the tour are lacking. We booked the tour in Portuguese, but the tour was entirely in Spanish (despite the majority of people in the van being Brazilian). The departure is very early, we were picked up at 5:50 at the hotel, then there is a stop for coffee on the way, around 7:30, a small place with few options, coffee around 3000 CLP. Afterwards we continued on the tour, with several stops, and wonderful landscapes, the Embalse El Yeso is very beautiful. After the tour, we stopped at a restaurant for lunch, an all-you-can-eat buffet with "barbecue" and dessert for 19000 CLP. There are no other options around, and the food isn't the best (I suggest bringing a snack). Next we go to Casa de Chocolate, which is a small chocolate and ice cream shop that requires a password to enter, it's not really worth it either (yummy gelato, but 3000 CLP a scoop). There is a stall selling the same ice creams at the back, without having to wait, but we only saw it on the way out (they said it was cheaper so it's worth checking beforehand). Finally, we returned to the same breakfast location to have our picnic. Don't create expectations, it's 1 glass of wine, juice or water per person, and a small cheese and salami board for the entire van. The tour is worth it, but I suggest preparing yourself for these details so you don't get frustrated. Review of: Tour Cajón del Maipo + Embalse el Yeso

review_text: We found the beach by following a small sign - it's really tricky to find the beach, but if you get there early enough you will avoid paying for parking. The water is really cold - everyone was wearing wetsuits, but there is a great little rental place with wetsuits, and different boards. I think you could get a surfing class too. Prices were reasonable and the owner spoke some English. There are toilets there for a small fee, and snacks are available. At the north end of the beach there is entry onto a long hike around the foreshore. It is quite well kept although very uneven - but the kids loved scrambling over the rocks and it also makes for some dramatic photos. There are several little bays where you can swim or paddle along the way, too. Of course the highlight is viewing the penguins on Cachagua Island - but if you want to go for a boatride for a closer look you will have to head to Caleta Zapallar for that.

review_text: We had a fantastic time visiting Villard. It was an easy drive from Santiago and Waze / Google Maps took us straight to the front door. Upon arrival, we were greeted by Thierry and his wife who's two sons run the winery. Thierry immediately announced that we were to get back into our car, complete with a bottle of wine and two glasses and took us on a tour of the vineyard explaining the wines they make, why they grow better in different areas and some history of the area. We then went back to the winery and had a tour of the production area and cellar. We finished the tour trying some of the fantastic wines. Thierry was enthusiastic and full of character and had an impressive knowledge of the region and wine making. We have visited wineries in Europe and South Africa, but found our experience in Chile (and in particular Villard) to be very personal and a great overall experience. We would highly recommend coming here whatever your knowledge of wine is or even if you just like drinking it!

review_text: Visited Quintay in April 2014 and am reminded of it now by The Big Blue on BBC which today was all about whales and included an account of the now largely defunct whaling industry. I am fascinated by whales and found this place haunting. On the quayside are rails that descend into the sea - and then you learn that these were used to haul the whale carcases on to the quayside for butchering. The old guy who takes the money for admission to the museum is a former whaler. He tells you that when the whaling station was at its height you could smell nothing but the foul stench of whale carcases for miles around. And romance was difficult when you couldn't remove the awful fish smell from your clothes and hands. There is something redeeming in the conversion of the old whale factories into a museum that records something of the history of the whaling industry. There are some gruesome photographs, but they show the truth of what was involved and can only help to reinforce the strength of feeling in support of whale conservation. If, like me, you are fascinated by these giants of the ocean, this small museum is well worth a visit. The bay is an interesting little place with beach restaurants that serve fish straight out of the sea, but be warned: there is only one road in and out, parking is limited and it is a very popular destination.

review_text: After a long day the day before visiting Salar de Tara and my daughter getting altitude sickness, we decided a relaxing day in the thermal springs would be perfect. It was! All agencies offer this but only some for the morning, which is much quieter. It really doesn't matter which agency you book with as you will all end up on the same buses (very cramped and old) and it is a standard price for the journey and then an extra 15.000CLP for entry on your arrival. Following a 30 minute bus journey, you arrive at the springs. There are 5 different thermal springs of different temperatures with walkways between each. There are toilets and change rooms with lockers but you need to bring your own padlock. Most people just carried their bags around with them and left them next to whatever pool they were in. Bring your own towels, snack and drinks as none of these are available on site (unless you are with Awasi!!). Also useful would be bathrobes (or something to slip on) and flip-flops. The tour usually provides for about 2 hours in the springs, which is long enough really. Then a 30 minute bus journey home. Be aware the springs are at 3200m, so above SPDA but for most, should be ok, especially if you have been higher on some of the other tours. I would recommend this trip on your final day or after you have done some longer day trips as it is incredibly relaxing. The water is so warm and clear. Some sun loungers would be nice but unfortunately the seating available is hard and uncomfortable.

review_text: The Atacama Desert is one of the world’s truly phenomenal natural wonders that stretches over 1,600 km providing stunning landscapes. It is among other things the driest non-polar desert, the only hot desert to receive less rainfall than polar deserts and the world’s largest fog desert. review_text: So many locals I met declared that Isla Negra was their favorite of the three homes of Pablo Neruda, I decided it had to be worth the day trip out there. The casa museo itself is quirky and filled with curios. Tons of nautical inspired collectibles—ship wheels, model ships, statues you'd find on a bow or stern of a boat; butterfly collections; shell collections—fill the rooms. The audio guide had some very illuminating stories on Neruda, which you could enjoy while gazing out windows overlooking the Pacific. Neruda was well-known as a “marinero en tierra,” or land-bound sailor that feared the ocean, and it’s easy to imagine this being the home that was nearest and dearest to his heart. I loved his ocean view bar--glass-enclosed, with friends' seats labeled, crowned with 200 bottles of liquor. What a cozy, intimate and absolutely unique home bar. Don’t neglect to spend time soaking it all in at El Rincon del Poeta, the onsite restaurant. I kicked back with a perfectly crisp sauvignon blanc from Casablanca Valle on the outdoor patio, while admiring the picture-perfect ocean view and basking in the warmth of the sun.

review_text: We took a tour with this company heading to Uyuni in Bolivia to see a series of its finest sights, including the salt flats. The company offers a 2.5 day tour ending in Uyuni or a 3.5 day tour where you are dropped back in San Pedro (Chile). The two of us had an excellent time and wish to recommend this company to other travellers. Our guide, Milton, was friendly, personable and conscientious - particularly at points where others in the group didn’t feel well because of the altitude. In particular we felt that Milton gave good information on the sights at each of the stops without overwhelming or inundating us with information. We also appreciated being dropped off in the car at our hotel in Uyuni when we chose to end the tour there. During the tour, the sights we saw were nothing short of stunning and we are so glad to have been able to see them. We recommend Sol Andino unreservedly as you can easily book in Chile while being able to rely on their Bolivian operation for expert guides. One thing we did notice from this tour is that it is advisable to make sure you know at least a little Spanish vocabulary beforehand: as two native English speakers with Spanish, we frequently found ourselves translating for the rest of the group as there seem to be no bilingual tour options for this tour route. Watch out - some of these can be marketed as bilingual tours and that is misleading. In addition, as it is necessary to buy Bolivian currency before crossing the border, it is also advisable to buy your Bolivianos somewhere other than San Pedro, where all businesses inflate the rate and you get stung in changing money, the same way you would at an airport. And be warned - the accommodation in Bolivia is very, very basic on these tours - although there don’t seem to be any luxurious options available, so give that some thought if you don’t think that standard will be for you. Assuming that’s not prohibitive, this route from San Pedro to Uyuni is well worth doing and we strongly recommend Sol Andino as the company to book with.

review_text: This bridge across the Quilo lagoon is 17 km west from Ancud town. It links the Guabun peninsula with the core of Chiloé island. Both the Corona lighthouse and the Ahui stronghold are located on Guabun. The bridge area is an excellent place to observe kingfishers as the water on both sides of the bridge is usually calm which means it is easy for the kingfishers to spot and target fish reaching the smooth surface. The Chilean variety of kingfisher is called "Martin Pescador". Unlike its cousins it has slightly raised crown feathers.

I arrived, picked up my package from the flashpackers and read through all the details. I couldn't have been more excited, and prepared. The trek itself is incredible and not something you really need a guide for. We stayed in the comfortable huts and ate yummy food the whole time and followed the itinerary provided. Im so happy I chose this company and will be using them in other countries in the future!

review_text: Awesome way to see the Southwest of Bolivia. We booked at the office in San Pedro and spoke with the boss Lionel. Ended up doing the 3D2N tour (200 USD pp). Same itenary as other reviews: minivan to the border with a few checkpoints (quite bureaucratic, remember the PDI paper from immigration into Chile) and then over into the 4X4 to start the adventure. Efrain/Chacho was our tourguide/driver/DJ/photographer and what an amazing guy he was. He was funny, calm and thoughtful and checked throughout if everybody was feeling OK. There is also oxigen in the car. You pass such amazing nature, it becomes quite overwhelming in 3 days. If you speak (some) Spanish, or someone in your group does, you will completely fine and will understand the explanations. Otherwise, ask/pay for an English speaking guide. We were glad we had a really nice group. We wanted to go even earlier into Salar de Uyuni to see the stars and Milky Way. Chacho arranged that no problem and without extra cost. It was amazing and a must see route in Bolivia. Only downside was the first night refugee/hostal. The warm water supply was not sufficient for all the people present and no heater in the room, so we ended up being really cold and tired. The second hotel is great!

review_text: I took a full day birding tour with BirdsChile in the Andes Mountains near Santiago, Chile. We birded at La Yerba Loca, Los Farellones, and El Nevado national parks. My guide, Carolina, was fun, enthusiastic, interesting, knowledgeable, and as excited to find Chile's bird species as I was. She took her time and was patient and relaxed and informative. We saw Andean Condors, Magellanic Great Horned Owls, Moustached Turcas, White sided Firestars, and many, many more native bird species. The national parks we birded at offered spectacular and stunning views of the Andes Mountains at 3000 meters (9,000 ft). The picnic lunch that Carolina provided had enough delicous food in it to feed a football team. I spent a wonderful and exciting day birding with BirdsChile and would highly recommend it to anyone who loves birding, or just loves discovering the flora, fauna, and natural beauty of a new country.

review_text: If you want to get to know Chile, it´s history and some of it´s art styles this is the place to be! About a ten minute walk away from the metro line 2, departamental station, this neigborhood with about 28 huge murals all painted on 4 floor buildings, has it all when it comes to urban art: Graffitti, politics, protest, history, nature, myths and hopes for the future. The amazing thing is that it´s just out there, free to visit in a typical residential neigborhood. We went on a saturday and there was NO ONE, we just strolled around the neighborhood enjoying one amazing mural after the other, from Chilean artists aswell as international ones. I would have given it 5 stars if there would have been more information to be found about each piece, now only some walls had a sign with the name of the piece and name of the artist, but there was nothing else to find, like a map or a info stand to get more information. Maybe that was the charm of it all, that it was not touristy and i guess I just have to find out more about the project online.

review_text: You may come with the bus from Valdivia, with the taxi, with a rented car or just by foot, but nothing prepares you for the scenery in which this old fort is placed. Naturally!, you must expect that a fort is well placed, but here the landscape and weather around are fascinating. Remember to wear rainproof clothes! From the entrance you could advert the landscape, placed on top of the hill of Morro Niebla, against the coastline is an excellent point of view both for enemies as well as for nature lovers. Starting from the vegetation around to the birds and the excellent walking pads made of steel, which do not disturb the beauty of the ancient buildings at all. Take your time to reflex the environment... look at the old structures and, when you come to the viewpoint for the cannons... take a look at the sea... maybe you are lucky and find the toninas (little dolphins!), sea wolves or even orcas and penguins. Best time to see marine life from above is the rise and down of the tide. The rains in spring and summer are copious and wonderful. In the fort is placed also an ancient lighthouse from 1900, which is also very imposing and well preserved. My advice, take at least 2 hours or more to visit the place with no rush.

review_text: As plazas go, this one is quite beautiful in the city’s location at the base of Chile and situated close to the majestic Strait of Magellan. The surrounding buildings each side of the plaza are from that era where the town’s prosperity saw mansions, banks and a beautiful Cathedral spring up. While we strolled around the square, we noticed the beautiful green conifers, the flowering garden beds, the impressive monument to Magellan, the souvenir stalls and where possibly our canine friends outnumbered the residents sitting around! One of the most notable buildings is the exclusive Club de la Unión and if you want a taste of the interior then a downstairs tavern is open to the public. The beautiful French - inspired Palacio Sara Braun (with museum), is a stunning heritage building reminiscent of this city’s quiet wealth. Sitting west of the plaza is Sacred Heart Cathedral Church where the single bell tower rises over the square. The church’s colour is a gorgeous creamy yellow and can be visited most days. Several restaurants, cafes and shops add a modern, urban flavour to the plaza but if you like remarkable architecture then you will enjoy walking in the historical heart of Punta Arenas - Plaza Muñoz Gamero. Enjoy your experience!

review_text: San Cristobal Hill is a very large area with more than one entrance. We took the funicular to go up the hill from the entrance we came in. The first stop on the funicular is the zoo, you can get off and explore this and then get back on another funicular when you're finished. Then the funicular takes you to the top where the statue of the Virgin Mary stands looking over Santiago. The statue is huge!!! There was prayer music being played over loud speakers. Wander around and see the crypts, churches and the view of Santiago (if there isn't a lot of smog) You can then walk down a walkway past the Crosses In The Path Of De Seven Last Words, unfortunately when we were there they had just blocked off that path and we had to go around. Then you can take the cable car down to the bottom of the hill. Or if you come in from that entrance you can do the cable car first then the funicular. There's also the option of hiking, with lots of trails. There were lots of dogs around the area, we were told they were strays that are quite placid, laying around, they don't bother people. A great area to spend some time

review_text: Our ship docked in San Antonio, Chile. Alejandro Villela helped us customize the tour that we wanted and which wines that we wanted to taste. Juan picked us up at the cruise port. The first winery that we visited was Casa Marin. We tasted 6 wines. We thought we would like the red best, but the Casa Marin guide wanted us to try their white wine, 2018 Sauvignon Blanc from Cipreses Vineyard. This was our favorite and we bought 3 bottles. We then went to Matetic Vineyards and tasted another 6 wines. The scenery was magnificent. We did not care for the wines here. Following this tasting we went to have a 4 course lunch with matching wines at El Emporio Restaurant. We had a lamb empanada, fish catch of the day, pork ribs, and a thousand layer cake. Juan then drove us back to the cruise port. It was a wonderful day and I would highly recommend it.

For know,let me talk about the 4 hikes we did at this beautiful national parkWe all increased our exercise routine based on the recommendation of our chilean friends leading our group. The hike to the glaciers was an easy introduction. About 5 miles . The second day we did the most challenging which was the hike to the French Valley. Besides being the longest(14miles) there was the pressure to get back so we would not miss the 6:30pm boat trip back to the other side of the lake and back to our camp.Third day the fauna trail where we were lucky to see the condors and plenty of guanagos on our trail. An afternoon small hike to the waterfall was the perfect end of the day. The hike to the base of the towers was left for last. Shorter than the french valley but more challenging. The day was cloudy and a misty rain was present but an amazing hike. Before you come here,take some long hikes on uneven terrain to help you get ready. Walking sticks are a great help in a couple of these trails.

review_text: We took a taxi from the tender port to the museum at a cost of $6,000 CH pesos or about $10 US. The Nao Victoria Museum has four full size replicas of ships of significant importance to Chile. What’s really neat about the Museum is that you can crawl all over the ships and even dress up in some of the garb of the era while playing with replicas of the weapons as well. The ships’ construction is true to their original versions and the full scale of the ships really drives home the confined spaces and conditions the crew and passengers would have experienced, in many cases for years at sea. The first and most impressive replica is the Victoria, a ship in Magellan’s fleet. The second was the oh so small modified whaling boat the John Caird that Shackleton used to travel 800 miles from where his men were stranded on Elephant Island in Antarctica to South Georgia Island to seek help, then finally onto Punta Arenas in another vessel to get reinforcements to actually recover his stranded men. The third is the Acuna, a ship that brought Chilean settlers to the Punta Arenas region, establishing Chilean sovereignty over the Straight of Magellan. The fourth ship, the HMS Beagle, the vessel Darwin travelled on from 1832 to 1836 with Robert Fitzroy as his Captain and the voyage on which he developed his theory of evolution, is still under construction, and although it won’t be finished until next year, you can still walk around its decks and appreciate the quality of construction and the care they are taking to produce an accurate copy. It’s the largest of the ships on display at 90 feet by 24 feet. Cost for the two and a half hours we spent there was 3,000 pesos or $5US each and they even feed us hot chocolate and provided a neat little audio “cube” that you took with you throughout your prowl that described the various parts and functions of the Victoria. When you know Shackleton's story, seeing the replica of the John Caird really brings home the almost impossible journey he and 5 others managed to make.

review_text: We did the day hikes to the base of Los Torres and from Centro to Las Cuernos. The trails are pretty but having arrived from Argentina's El Calafate and El Chalten where we had been hiking for the past couple of days, we were not that wowed with the scenery on the hike to Los Torres' base (which also happens to be tougher than the day-long hikes we've been on in Argentina). Hopefully other parts of the 'W' circuit are nicer. Park rangers in Chile are also less friendly and helpful than the ones in Argentina. Everything is also overpriced in Torres Del Paine, from food to accommodations to activities. We definitely enjoyed ourselves more in El Calafate and El Chalten. Accommodation and transport operators hold a monopoly in TDP national park, so expect sky-high prices and average service and quality. The 'W' Circuit is supposed to be amazing (we didn't attempt the entire circuit because of time constraints) but if you're in TDP just for day hikes, all I'm saying is that there may be better choices elsewhere. Tip: While the map and guides tell you the hike from Las Torres Hotel to the base of the mountain is only 4.5 hours one way, it's really more like 5.5 hours because the trail is so crowded and you end up having to stop for hikers passing from the other direction every other minute. So make sure to give yourself plenty of time to complete the trail, and more if you want to stop for lunch and snacks as well.

review_text: When you ask the average person (including this reviewer before visiting this museum) to list the significant civilizations of pre-Colombian Central and South America you will likely get a short list that includes the Mayans, the Aztecs, and the Incas. The Chilean Museum of Pre-Colombian Art dispels this notion in decisive fashion. Inaugurated in 1981 and extensively renovated in 2014, the institution’s collection contains over 3,000 items categorized into almost 100 different groups spanning 10,000 years. It is a virtual treasure trove of irreplaceable artistic objects. I visited twice here on consecutive days at the end of my week in the country. The building consists of three main sections: a lower floor exhibit covering the history of Chile Before Chile,” a larger second floor experience covering the rest of the Americas (minus upper North America), and a smaller rotating exhibit on the ground floor displaying “daily wear and tear” and its effects on indigenous artifacts. “Chile Before Chile” is divided geographically; artifacts from the Far North, Near North, Central, and Southern zones are grouped and include items as diverse as neonatal mummies and wooden flutes. The second-floor collection is more extensive, covering a larger geographic area, and included an even more varied set of objects: Mayan ceramic vases, Shaman wooden “purging spatulas,” Vicus ceramic house models, etc. The rotating exhibit was in a single room and fairly brief, while a small gift shop rounded out the experience. In summary, this was an equally memorable and exhausting experience. First and most importantly, as stated in the introduction it truly opened my eyes to the variegated groups of people that inhabited this part of the Americas in the past. Most of the items on display were simply beautiful to look at and English translations were thankfully the norm and not the exception. Second, the museum does an above average job of organization, with the groups displayed geographically in eight rooms with timelines shown for temporal context. My only suggestion to the staff would be to have a phone app or audio guide to make the place easier to navigate for those with limited time. In any case, this museum should be included on even the most cursory visit to Santiago. Review of: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino Admission Ticket

We tried calling the establishment for more information several times but they never picked up. On the day, we took a taxi up to the Observatory and as we arrive at the entrance we are told that we have to have physical tickets and our reservation means nothing. We are told that this keeps happening and to turn around and go all the way back to Vicuña. We were quite upset as this would mean we would miss the tour we had booked but he reassured us and said we could go on the next one and that there’s a free transfer for us at the bottom. There was no logic to why we needed physical tickets even though our booking had generated a QR code. We finally get to the office where tickets are 12.000 pesos (not 7.000 as previous reviews state) and the transfer isn’t free it’s an extra 5.000 per person for a trip we had just done. The woman was rude but we explained our situation to the transfer guy and he was understanding but said his service was separate from them altogether that he essentially is a taxi driver. We go back to the office to speak to boss. Us four girls start to explain everything that had happened and tried to reason with him, because if we had known it was an extra 20.000 to get physical tickets 3 of us would have stayed at the observatory waiting. He was possibly the rudest and most disrespectful man I have met in my LIFE. He clearly did not care about customer service and his one and only sim was to scam us and take advantage of tourists. As he continued to call us liars and blaming us for their misinformation and communication problems, we had decided that the situation had gotten so aggressive that we no longer wanted to support this business. Our friend had gone one hour beforehand and texted us saying that is was NOT WORTH IT. Turns out you aren’t even allowed into the observatory anyway? It’s just a name and there’s someone who talks you through the different type of stars. We were so glad we decided not to go and felt sorry for our friend who wasted a total of 65USD on their scam. I highly recommend nobody goes to this place as apart from NOT BEING AN OBSERVATORY they will SCAM you for as much money as they possibly can with TERRIBLE CUSTOMER SERVICE. There are other observatories in the area that would be a better option.

review_text: This hike was amazing!!! I knew I had a full day lay over in Santiago since my flight was at 11.30 PM. Therefore, some days before, I contacted Coigüe expeditions to help me make the best out of the day I had. They were super responsive and provided me with all information I needed to prepare for the hike. Nicolas came to pick me up exactly as scheduled with water and food for the day, and drove me the the heart of the Andes, close to the border with Argentina. He is a very nice and knowledgeable guide, and really passionate about hiking and the mountains of his country. The hike is not hard, as you will be walking in a valley at more or less the same altitude. However, you will be hiking between 2500-2900 meters/or 8200-9500 feet, so, if you are not already used to that, be prepared to find yourself catching up with your breath every now and then. The place is really beautiful. The valley is really green and hosts a lot of Andean birds. The glacier is really impressive. I would definitely recommend Nicolas and Coigüe Expeditions to everybody who loves outdoor activities, sports and adventure, and to whoever wants to be completely surrounded by the fantastic nature of Chile. Review of: Juncal Andean Park: Hiking over a Glacial Tongue Thank you very much for recommending us, Matteo. We are very happy you liked this hiking experience to the encounter of largest glacier of Central Chile, which hangs from almost 6,000 meters above sea level. We send you a huge hug and we hope to see you again to go out for more adventures.

review_text: This is a cathedral but it is not any particularly grander than other catholic churches in the neighborhood. The one in Peru gives you the impression that Cathedral is the grandest in Lima. This one in Chile went through fire and earthquakes and it was rebuilt 2-3 times in different stages. The 2 towers were added after the church was rebuilt at a later stage. The Cathedral has people there attending most of the time, I went in there 2-3 times during my stay in Chile, they always had people there (not as tourists) and the confession booths had priests attending also. I would say, this is a more functional Cathedral than a symbolic building for the catholic church.

review_text: Situated at the Quinta Normal Park with a metro station carried the same name makes it easy to access. The museum is FREE so expect a big crowd everyday. I was here to see the 3 Rongo rongo inscriptions from Easter Island but due to the earthquake happened recently, there were cracks on the ceilings so the 2nd floor that displayed Rongo rongo was closed. But other than that it's still worth a visit. The museum has a big collection of animal specimens from all over Chile that categorized geographically and according to their habitat. It's especially good for those who has a short time in Chile or come during the wrong season that you can't see the animal. The museum has collection from Atacama desert, Mediterranean Santiago, Andean down to Antarctica. At the center of hall you will see the skeleton of a whale, which is the icon of the museum. And you can see the evolution of whale from land to sea. Besides that you will see some big mammals from around the world like Bengal tiger, American bison and Borneo Orangutan. There are a little bit of cultural antiques as well, especially the Easter Island Rapa Nui collection. Thank you for your comments!

review_text: Getting here in involves an early start, in order to see the geysers at dawn, when the cold air makes the steam, from the geysers, more visible This is "the third largest geyser area in the world", which sounds good but only refers to the acreage and not the quality of the geysers; "Old Faithful" or Rotorua it is not. It was cold when we arrived, -7C, and we could watch the sun rise as we wandered around the geysers. The geysers are mainly like bubbling pools of water, with steam being the most obvious feature. We did find some where the water was spat up to about 2 metres into the air but it took time to witness even such modest events. Although there are a lot of people there, they soon disperse so that we didn't get in each others' way. Photography was more difficult than I had anticipated, mainly because so much of it was so unspectacular. We did get to see some interesting sights on the way back to San Pedro but I am not sure that it was worth the effort of such an early start.

review_text: A good tour which you cannot miss when you are at Puerto Rio Tranquilo. The colour of the marble looks so good in several ways that you view it. Very nice. There are a lot of agencies at the river bank which offer the tour. It costs 10.000 per person and it doesn't really matter which agency you go to. They all do the same: navigate to the caves, visit 3 spots of Marble Caves, go into these caves with the boat, navigate back. I advise you to go in the morning, because the low sun shines into the caves and the colour of the marble is much more beautiful. Most tours leave at 8 am or 4 pm. They do not go when the lake is too rough due to the wind or when it is raining. Have fun!

review_text: This museum is an obligatory visit for anyone remotely interested in justice, equality and human rights around the world, as well as the history of Latin America. The Chilean coup and the dictatorship that followed are emblematic of some of the deepest flaws of the 20th century. A visit here confronts you with the suffering caused by the coup in a very personal, devastating manner. However, there is a lack of complete clarity in terms of an explanation of the political and economic background that led to this terrible event. For visitors from the United States in particular, I found that the museum glossed over the participation of the CIA, Kissinger and the infamous domino theory in the orchestration of the coup. Just as Chileans must confront and recognize their past, so should the international community and especially the United States.

review_text: We almost got snowed in at 4,800 meters in the Andes. I want to start by clarifying that the score is for the agency and NOT for the guides or the places visited. I would say that almost all of the tours we did (Valle de la Luna, Piedras Rojas, Laguna Cejar, and Ruta de Salares) were worth it; they are wonderful places and the guides were excellent. Only the astronomical tour seemed too massive and lacking in dedication, and our astrophotos came out with the Milky Way cut off because they didn't move the camera with the movement of the sky. The low score is due to something particular but, in my opinion, serious: on June 24th, we learned that a snowstorm had been announced in the mountains, and on June 25th we had scheduled the Ruta de Salares tour, which climbs to 4,800 meters. They recommended that we try to change it. We went to the agency to try to change it to a lower-altitude tour and were denied the option because "it was too short-term." When we insisted on the risk of weather conditions, we were told it would be no problem. On the day of the tour we almost got trapped up there in the snowstorm. News reports show that at least 59 people had to be rescued the next day. If we made it to the bottom, it was thanks to our guide (Javier), who had an excellent handling of the situation and the path. We couldn't see anything at all and we had to go off the road a few times to get down. The worst part is that when we filed a complaint with the agency, we weren't even apologized. They claimed there was no error on their part since it was the company's policy not to suspend work unless instructed to do so by the Carabineros. I understand that it's impossible to predict the weather, and I didn't ask for the tour to be cancelled, but rather to be allowed to change it because I didn't want to risk getting stuck up there, as could very well have happened (and happened to other tourists). I think if the agency's policy is to put passengers at risk, it would be worth reviewing the company's policy or at least acknowledging the mistake and apologizing.

review_text: While visiting Chile for the 2019 solar eclipse, my family and I decided to experience a bit more of this wonderful and ecologically diverse country. In particular, we wanted to see the araucaria trees that grow in the Araucanía region to the south of Santiago. The images we had seen online were simply unreal. My wife looked up tour agencies that would take us into Nahuelbuta National Park, and that's how we found Weñimahuida. What followed was a truly magical day of getting to know this stunningly beautiful and ancient forest. Our guide, Sebastian, was very informative, helpful, genuinely invested in the future of the park and his town, and just an all-around good guy. The tour he had in store was just the right mix of seeing as much of the park as we could at a reasonable pace that allowed for contemplation and didn't exhaust our two kids. Sebastian also provided valuable information about the flora, fauna, and history of the area. In the end it was everything we had hopped for and literally more, as he even dropped is off at a local eatery that was also quite good. If you're looking to see an underrated and less well-known corner of Chile, Nahuelbuta National Park is the place to go and Weñimahuida is definitely the way to do it. Review of: Nahuelbuta National Park Tour

review_text: Being from San Francisco my wife and I are accustomed to the big cabernets of Napa Valley and the pinot and chardonnay from Sonoma. The San Antonio valley is similar to Sonoma but with closer proximity to the ocean and a more distinct minerality. San Antonio valley is strongly influenced by limestone in the soil, you can see it in the hillsides. This gives Casa Marin's wine a distinct flavor that we haven't found anywhere else. It also helps that the wines are well made, showcasing the unique land without overpowering the wine. Almer was our tour guide and showed us around the property. The building itself is unassuming along with the wine cellar. We didn't get a chance to the see the small town of Lo Abarca, but the surrounding countryside is beautiful. The tasting room is upstairs with a large window providing a great view. We were poured three wines, and ones that stood out were the 2009 Pinot and 2010 Syrah. We also tried the Sauvignon Blanc which was very unique, it showcased San Antonio's unique soil well. I am a sucker for a cool climate Syrah so we bought that and the Pinot. Almer also provided some locally made olive oil during the tasting which was flavorful and had some bite. Overall a very personal and pleasant experience. However, be prepared to drop some cash. The wine is not cheap, and that is not just comparing it to Chilean wine, but the US as well. Almer told us that the founder and winemaker, Maria Luz, wanted to create a premium wine and charge a premium price. She succeeded on both fronts. The tour fee was also around 30 dollars per person and not waived with the purchase of wine. But was it worth it? Of course! This is one of Chile's "smaller" boutique producers and the wine is excellent. I admire Maria's tenacity and bravery starting Casa Marin in a valley that previously didn't have any wineries. It is worth a visit.

review_text: We agreed to meet Miguel at 5 am. From the moment we met, his treatment was cordial and in his truck we began the tour. His ability to drive impeccably even on winding roads is very surprising, while his eyes and ears are attentive to any indication that nature gives him to show and explain to us, and at the same time his mind is putting together for us a living story about ecology. of the pumas, the ecosystem, the landscape of Torres del Paine, the environmental history of the region and the conservation actions that have been carried out in the area. Ah! And he also coordinated the team that was in other vehicles by radio and joked with them in an atmosphere that relaxed us a lot, all at the same time! At around 10 am we managed to see a puma for a few seconds... then, we found a very clear footprint, and we stayed at rest with that satisfaction. But upon resuming the route in the afternoon, Miguel detected a reclining puma. We spent several hours watching him while he dozed, and every time he raised his head or moved his tail we got excited taking photos. Miguel only said: we have to wait, he's going to get up and we'll see what he does. When he finally began to walk Miguel knew how and where we should position ourselves to be able to respectfully observe the majestic animal. In addition, his help with the observation and photography equipment was great, he is a great nature photographer and does not hesitate to share his experience and extensive knowledge. It was difficult to have to leave because the transportation was waiting for us, and for a long time we continued to feel the adrenaline (Pumaína, as Miguel rightly says) of the encounter. They are a biologist, with a doctorate in ecology and natural resource management, and I can say that this experience has been the best example that I have been able to witness of biological conservation and respect for nature that I have known in Latin America. I feel deeply grateful to the entire Iso100 Outdoor team, and especially to Miguel, not only for allowing us to live this experience, but for the committed, responsible and respectful work for the preservation of this magnificent feline and its habitat. If I ever have the opportunity to return, it would be to spend more days under the guidance of Iso100 Outdoor, in this paradise on our planet that is Torres del Paine. My total recommendation to the company, since their work and experience are invaluable.

review_text: We decided we wanted to see smaller/more local wineries on our last day in Santiago, so booked a full-day tour the day before with Uncorked to see the nearby Casablanca Valley wineries; we were happy they had space for us, and found the tour to be excellent; Uncorked seems to focus on small to medium sized wineries, which is ideal, these are often hard to tour otherwise, and provide a very authentic and interesting experience. The small winery was called recova and was quirky and fun, with a notable setting amid rolling hills. The final winery was where we had lunch. a much bigger operation (but very good food), whose name I forget. At Recova we even got to taste wine in the process of fermentation which was new to me - interesting to try a couple stages. One nice thing about these tours is, unlike most of California tours, the pours were not restricted - they would leave the bottles out, so if you liked one in particular (or 5 in particular), you could have more. Overall, we had an excellent time and would definitely recommend Uncorked. Review of: Best Wine Tasting in Santiago

review_text: My wife and I wrapped up a three-week trip through Argentinian Patagonia and Torres del Paine with a week-long surf vacation in Pichilemu, Chile. While Patagonia was breathtaking, our time with Ismael was actually the most memorable part of the trip. If you’re looking for a surf trip, especially one that’s private, tailored, and perfect for first-timers, I can’t recommend Ismael enough. It’s an experience you’ll never forget!

review_text: These pools are located in a lush canyon valley about half hour from San Pedro de Atacama. The drive would seem to resoundingly confirm there's no water anywhere around as the terrain is barren (yet beautiful) but devoid of life. Then as you drive higher you start seeing a little bit of fauna and then some cactuses and then you cross an almost dry river bed with a small creek in the middle. None of that will prepare you for the massive amount of water that is pouring out some underground springs heated by some distant volcanic activity. review_text: Myself and two friends went on the Isluga excursion. We were picked up at 3:30 am outside of our hotel and joined a group that already included 6 others and our wonderful guide Mauricio. I noticed he was the same man who had booked our trip the previous day -- he is one hard working dude! Our first stop were the geysers which we saw at sunrise and then had breakfast. Afterward we stopped at a few Altiplano towns and then walked through a lush lagoon full of flamingos and many other birds. Volcan Isluga was fuming in the background. We had lunch in Colchane and saw the geoglyphs ending with the Giant of Atacama. Mauricio was extremely knowledgable and told us much about the ecology and culture of the Altiplano and its peoples. Just FYI the explanations were entirely in Spanish, though I think Mauricio may also have been able to explain in English. Highly recommend!

review_text: I think my review would be a lot different if I had the typical experience....Cejar had been closed for the previous 4 days due to road conditions, so when it opened back up finally, we rushed there and arrived on the early side. I think a lot of people assumed it was still closed, because we had it all to ourselves for a while, which was awesome! The laguna itself is beautiful, I'm not much of a beach/swimming person, but it was fun to float around briefly in that setting. I say briefly because especially as a fair skinned person, being forced to go in with no sunscreen meant a rush job. And I still got HORRIBLY burnt. I haven't had a sunburn like that in a decade. It may or may not be worth noting that Cejar is not the one you actually can swim in, it is another one nearby. It was quite expensive, especially given how long I could stay without getting 3rd degree burns, and the shower was really appreciated since the feeling of salt on my skin is a sensation I loath. The woman working the bathhouse hovered over everyone, glowering and yelling in spanish, so that took away from it a bit. I took well less than the max 3 minutes....but left as soon as possible because she was literally standing 3 feet away just staring and glowering. I think this is as close to a prison shower experience as I'll ever have, so I guess thanks for that ;) It was worthwhile for me, especially having it all alone for a short time - as we were leaving the buses started pouring in, and I'm sure that experience is a very different one, unfortunately.

review_text: We highly recommend this small group star gazing tour! You must book in advance by going to their office in Vicuña near the town plaza, they open at 10am. Once booked they will ask you to report to that booking office to meet prior to your tour and drive via their mini bus to the observatory.Our tour was at 8 pm wear flat shoes and be sure to take a sweater as it gets cool in the Mountains. Take some water as well it is a few hours in total. Erik was our guide he is one of the owners and a very knowledgeable astronomer! His knowledge alone was well worth the price of the tour! No question was left unanswered ! We had some lovely people on our tour and really found out so much about the stars planets and more! The view of the Milky Way was incredible! Something we will never forget coming from the USA! The Southern Cross shone bright in the night sky! You do drive up into the Andes on a mountain road for about 30 minutes. The driver was excellent thank goodness he knew the road line the back of his ‘Ande’ Once we arrived we had a full two hours of star gazing! The guest were all amazed by the beauty of the sky! The 16 inch automatic telescope was fabulous! We took turns to look after it was set on various attractions! Along with very good information about each item we were to view. The knowledge of Erik was like the universe ..... vast! Tours were in Spanish ,French and English. There is an age limit of no children under 16 I believe you may wish to check on that with them. All in all it was the most amazing experience. Be aware that they don t do this tour on nights with heavy cloud and a full moon! Don’t miss out on this ! The trip of a lifetime!!

review_text: While in Arica, apart from going to the beach, there's just no better thing to do for a tourist (in my opinion) than to come up this hill with a "very spacious" viewing area on the top. And apart from the great "stretching views" of the city & the sea and the close views (just down below on one side) of the colorful shipping containers at the Port & the old Spanish island Ex-Isla Alacran (no longer an island with a connecting land bridge now but still "kind of charming" to look at from above), there are also: a big Chilean flag (pretty awesome really to see this "quite sizeable" flag at a close-up although I also noticed some wears & tears which may be due to how long it has been on this hilltop!), a military museum where you can learn a fair bit about the 1880's War of the Pacific from its displays mostly of arms used in that war including some cannons displayed outdoors near the museum (where there are actually also some big info plates for the "comprehensive timeline" of this area from the prehistoric times to the colonial time to the present), and a Christ statue facing the sea on a fairly-high pedestal (which in comparison to the two other Christ statues I got to is about the same size as Cristo Blanco in Cusco & about a third the size of Christ the Redeemer in Rio). The hill is "fairly steep" but really it just takes about 15 minutes through a stairway followed by something like a "winding ramp" (which is the part of the climb I actually found somewhat uncomfortable for both going up & coming down and where I wished had just been stairs all the way to the top). And down below in the vicinity of this hill, just at a short walk from the bottom of the stairway is the small museum of Chinchorro mummies (to see through a glass floor), then further down the street are San Marcos Cathedral (a lovely white-and-brown building although not much to see inside) and the "shopping cluster" of a number of streets lined with all kinds of shops (with some nice souvenir shops among them).

review_text: I was a bit taken aback when I read the other reviews of this park as I don't think it does it justice. As others mentioned, the park has a number of hiking trails that are well marked, with boardwalks and plaques with information on fauna. The trails are relatively easy-going - 45 min to 1 hour loops, at most - and we had no issues doing the hikes with our three kids, so it is definitely geared to people of all physical abilities. For a Chilean national park, this park has a lot of infrastructure - places to eat, some small museums, camping, etc. - which makes it an easy visit for most people. The beach (which you can either walk to or drive to - we drove as it was too far for the kids to walk) is next to a native reserve and was amazing. It is extremely wide, clean and wild - we had a wonderful picnic there. What was even better than both the hiking trails and the beach was a nearby fossil beach. Instead of turning right from the main road to get to the national park, take a left and follow the road to the VERY END. I mean the very end of the road!!! You will think you're going the wrong way as the road turns into a pretty rough track (4x4 vehicle is a must), and ends at a fence. On closer inspection the fence is actually a gate that can be opened, and is only there to keep the horses in the fields. Go through the gate, across the fields and follow the marked trails towards the ocean (about 30-45 min of easy hiking), where you will end up at a beautiful rock beach covered in fossils. The fossils are mostly shells, but we also found some plant and fish fossils. There were also two mysterious memorials there from 1960 and 2010, likely from tsunamis that followed the big earthquakes that happened in those years. The place was deserted, even at high season - we only saw one family that was returning with their gear after a camping trip there. The river that meets the ocean at this beach seems to be full of large fish. Definitely a must see! Our kids were thrilled by the hike and the fossils, and it was truly off the beaten track which made it even better!

review_text: I was traveling with a friend in San Pedro and we wanted to go for a 3 days tour to Uyuni. After many terrifying stories about drunk drivers we asked for some opinions to some people in our hostel. More than one told us to go with World White Travel. The best choice we could make. Casimiro is the best driver/guide you can find in this trip. He is very professional and always ready 5 minutes before the meeting time. Here is a summary of the tour: Day 1: departure from San Pedro at 8 am to reach the border at 9 am. At the border we started the real trip with Casimiro. We went to Laguna Blanca, Laguna Verde, the Geysers and Laguna Colorada (surely the best place). The first night is very tough, with no electricity sleeping in a cold place at 4900 Mts of altitude, but this is part of the adventure. Day 2: Casimiro gave us two options: option 1 the usual your for this day; option 2: an amazing tour of rocks with basically a very few agencies on the way. We all selected option 2 and it was a perfect choice. The second night we slept in a salt hostel with warm showers and comfortable beds. Day 3: we reached the salt flat to take the famous pictures in a white desert. Casimiro was always willing to take us pictures and gave advices for the cool video we recorded. After a nice visit of the "island" in the middle of the salt flat, we reached Uyuni where Casimiro dropped us off in the World White Office in Uyuni. Even if we finished the trip the company helped us to find the best way to reach La Paz and gave us the opportunity to leave our luggage there for few hours. The food was good, the car comfortable and Casimiro always to help us when we had some problems with the altitude (it is common). Everything was perfect. An advice: don't go for the cheapest offer just to save 10$. This could be the worse experience of your life since it depends a lot on the guide.

review_text: I can't think of a better way to get acquainted with a brand new city! review_text: If you are looking for a place to party, this is not your choice, however, Patio Bellavista is located in the heart of Santiago's Bohemian District, were Chilean high society, middle class and working class party and have fun 365 days a year. This place has several restaurants and pubs to spend a good time within several possibilities, from a romantic dinner to a drink and finger food night with friends. Please bare in mind that Chileans go to dinner and party very late, so expect restaurants and pubs to be absolutely deserted before 9pm and utterly packed after 10pm. A taxi from providencia or Las Condes should not exceed USD10-15 and it should take you less than 10 mins to get there. Santiago Metro usually closes before 11pm so it might be a good idea to get there by metro and leave in a taxi. The gastronomic possibilities in this venue can be as diverse as it can get, you can get an Irish style burger in Dublin Irish Pub, to a delicious Peruvian ceviche. The place got private parking and has several ATM's in case you run out of cash.

review_text: "Quite impressive" was the spectacle of the guard-change ceremony involving a sizeable contingent of foot soldiers (with rifles on one side of their bodies), about ten mounted soldiers (with rifles across their backs & lances in their hands) and a music band playing some lively music (actually including the song YMCA); and yes the best thing about this ceremony I would say is its being held on the "open grounds" (right in front of the Palace) with "no iron bars" of the fence to look through unlike the one in Lima where it's just impossible to get nice pics having to look through those bars of the fence (and where I didn't see any horses either which just was "not as great" a spectacle as the one seen here). So it was a Sunday that I saw this ceremony which started at about 11 am for about half an hour, and it was actually my second day in a row at the Palace having to come back since there's no ceremony held on Saturdays. As for around the Palace itself, just outside the Palace's front grounds is an area with a "spacious lawn" & walkways where there are also about 5 or 6 statues of the prominent figures like some of the past presidents (including that of Salvador Allende who was deposed by the military coup) and where I also saw some sidewalk art exhibit (mainly of big posters depicting great sightseeing sites of the country); and yes also be sure not to miss the back side of the Palace where there's like a big "reflecting pool" with a number of small fountains in it (really just beautiful & spacious grounds back there to see from the sidewalks on 3 sides right outside the grounds) and where there's also an underground cultural center with 3 levels where on the bottom level are 2 display galleries with one across the floor from the other (and with both showcasing "horse-related" displays like model horses & riders, beautiful saddles, some shining accessories made of silver or such, nice paintings & photos with horses in them, etc. at the time of my visit back in January). Coming by metro, Plaza de Armas Station (Line 5) is where to get off from which it's just a 10-to-15-minute walk after exiting the Plaza from its south side (first along the "pedestrian street" lined with some shops and also outdoor vendors of souvenirs & such for 3 blocks followed by a right turn which is just the way straight to the front grounds of the Palace).

review_text: Had the wind been over 30 knots, we would still have been on the boat. We made it!!! The wind was blowing, it had been snowing during the night and rain early morning. Bundled up we stepped into the rubber zodiacs and zoomed off to step ashore. As we landed a wave crashed over the stern and we quickly picked up our feet so not to fill our shoes with water... Up the stairs then faced the wind which was clipping along at 30 knots. Looking out to the rough seas that have sank many a boat was awesome . The lighthouse family is there for a year. We trudged to the top of the lighthouse and out to the memorial before heading back to the transport boats. Hope you make it to the top on your trip.

review_text: My wife and I planned a 2-day tour of the Casablanca Valley at the end of a 2.5 week trip to Argentina and Chile. Our agent recommended that we include a stop at Kingston Family Vineyards. I did some research and saw that they have been producing exceptional wines, so we decided to give it a try. Coming from a wine-producing area of the U.S., we have taken many winery tours and have done lots of tastings. So we thought we knew what to expect. But we were in for a surprise. From the moment that we arrived and met the assistant winemaker (Alejandra) to the superb vineyard and winery tour given by Judith, the experience was fantastic and far exceeded our expectations. But best of all, we enoyed a private tasting at the end where we got to taste some fabulous Kingston Family wines (the Pinot Noir was my favorite, but the Syrah was also great!). We would highly recommend that anyone who is travelling to the Casablanca Valley be sure to make a point of going to Kingston. You will remember the experience and you will love the wine!
