review_text: We have been recommended Ivan of Arica Unlimited by three different persons when looking for a great guide to take us to discover the Arica region. We were so glad to meet Ivan who is probably the most knowledgeable guide of the area and has a real passion for the region and its fauna and flora (he can also organise birdwatching tours). We went on a 4-day trip with him, starting from our hotel in Arica (Apacheta hôtel) from where he picked us up on the first day. His new jeep wangler was ideal to discover the region (don’t self drive in the region as the roads and not easy to drive on and you are likely to miss out in the many secret places only a local guide can take you to) and Ivan has plenty of stories, anecdotes and interesting facts about the Andes’ nature, history, the Aymara people and their traditions, etc. Here is a short overview of our tour: on day 1 we went to pick up fresh fruits and vegetables at the Arica market, went to see the museum were you can find the oldest mummies of the world (7000 years old!), went birdwatching in the wetlands before properly hitting the road and reaching the Reserva Nacional Las Vicunas to reach Putre at the end of the day where we spent our first night in a nice local hotel. On day two, we crossed the Parque Nacional Lauca, stopped by the Lake Chungara and its impressive surrounding volcanoes, took a nice walk on Diablo marka crater - stopped by many little mountain villages, and discovered the impressive Salar de Surire Salt Lakes where we had a lovely lunch in the sun! We then drove through the Parque Naciona Volan Isluga and spent the night in a nearby village. On day 3 we started by visiting an area with giant cactus, then we went to a nice place where we swam in thermal waters and got to see the geysers. It was only the three of us which made it really special! We then drove into the desert where we spotted some ancient Inca hieroglyphics and visited the abandoned city of Humberton. On the last day, we went to the Red Lagoon where we had breakfast before taking a great walk in the canyon following the river. We then started making our way back to Arica. It was a fantastic and really off the beaten tracks journey full of history and nature and that we are not ready to forget! Thanks again Ivan for your awesome service and good mood during the entire trip!

review_text: I've fished with Will twice on the Rio Claro and both times enjoyed success catching healthy, hard-fighting rainbow trout. Although late summer might not be the ideal time to fish the Claro, Will knows the best spots to pull out finicky fish any time of the year. His relationship with landowners allows him to get to the best spots, off the beaten path, and in some truly majestic areas. Imagine pulling a wild rainbow out of a deep, crystal clear pool under the gaze of a snow-capped 15,000-foot volcano. Did I mention you won't see another soul on the water? If the fishing may only be matched by the scenery, it's Will's knowledge and demeanor that really ties the trip together. I had as much fun learning new techniques and tips from Will as I did pulling out fish from the ample runs, cuts, and eddies that dominate trout habitat in the Claro. I would definitely recommend staying in Will's lodge and making a weekend (or week!) out of your fishing trip. The food, wine and hospitality are remarkable and if you are still itching to fish after hitting the Claro, or want to get some casts in before embarking on your trip, a small tributary of the river flows right through the lodge's backyard. I've caught many rainbows meters away from my room! If you live in Santiago or are visiting Chile and want a legit Andean experience, I highly recommend booking a trip with Will and Andes Adventures. The fishing is great, the scenery spectacular and the guide service is top-class. Will has found a gem of a river and has made a living sharing it with people from all over the world. Take advantage!

review_text: If you’re reading this, it’s likely that you’re weighing your options on how to schedule a trip to Torres del Paine. Let me save you valuable time and cut to the chase— book via ChileTour and you’ll start and ends at the Garden Domes & Cabins. Cecilia is fast in responding, detail oriented and very professional. She answered all of my many questions, as I was a solo traveler who likes to know every aspect of my trip. The Garden Domes are unique and quite fun. Everyone dines in a dome, there is a dome with couches and such to hang out in, and if you want, you can book to have a room with a dome. I chose a cabin instead, and was delighted to have it overlooking the sea and mountains. The food at the Garden Domes and with Chiletour is outstanding and plentiful. You’ll enjoy it, and you can’t go hungry. The staff here is welcoming, friendly, and willing to help in any way. Richie, the owner, is the creative genius behind this operation and his latest addition is 4 tiny houses that are right outside the park. After you hike to the base of Torres del Paine the first night, it’s fabulous to come back knowing you’ll have a great meal and a great night in a comfortable bed without having to tent or check into a refugio (neither of those are bad, but it’s really nice to just have a known entity when you’re weary after a long first day in the park). Richie is cool under pressure, accommodating, and speaks 7 languages! Liz and Gonzalo work the reception desk and are delightful as well. They helped me add onto my stay, as I had a kayaking trip after TdP. I liked the Garden Domes so much that I booked them as an extension, forfeiting a non-refundable room elsewhere that I had previously booked. This is saying a lot, as I like to save anywhere I can! For me, it was worth knowing I’d be comfortable, have a peaceful atmosphere and I didn’t even know about the awesome hot tub they have until Richie suggested I try it out. What a great surprise! Now, about ChileTour. You have numerous options. I chose the classic tour. This was right for me because it was my first time trekking, and also because a I wanted to add the ice hike. Some did the 4 day “active” tour, which is fine, but they couldn’t add on the ice hike (which was SPECTACULAR) and I felt they rushed the last day (which in the classic is broken into 2 days). The active might be right for you, if you don’t mind less stops the last day, and you don’t want to ice hike. There was also a small group who did day hikes and stayed in the tiny house. Though they didn’t see as much of the park, they didn’t have to carry a full pack on any of their hikes. Whichever you choose, it’s great to know that you’ll be taken care of, treated like family, known by name when you return for your celebratory dinner and be sure to check out the hot tub! Now save all the review reading, do yourself a favor, book ChileTour with Garden Domes and Cabins, then relax. You’re in excellent hands. Have a great adventure at TdP. It’s breathtakingly beautiful. It is really helpful for new trekkers looking for an adventure. Hope to see you soon in Patagonia :) Kind regards from all the ChileTour team

review_text: Cerro San Cristóbal is located in the Parque Metropolitano, an area which is very popular with both Santiaguinos as well as tourists. You can ride your bike all the way up to the summit of the Cerro, and once you get there, your eyes will have the whole city before them, so it's worth going up. You can reach the summit either by taking the Funicular, or by taxi, or on a bike, or on foot. I'd recommend taking the paved road because if you take the different paths, you run the risk of being mugged. At the top, there is a small chapel where you can sit and pray, if you are a believer; there are also several shops that sell Mote con Huesillos, a good beverage that we Chileans like to drink on hot days.

review_text: Spectacular views!!! There's no cel or internet signal so it's the best place to disconnect from the world. I went in the beginning of March, it was almost empty so it was even more relaxing. We went by car but I have heard there're vans tha take you the 30 min ride from the nearest city to the park on high season, if not, the taxis are expensive. There is nowhere to buy food or drinks around so be prepared and take a cooler and lots of food beforehand, just a few little fishermen restaurants close by. Each camping site has a little structure to put the tent underneath and a little barbecue site, there's no electricity, bathrooms are nearby, they're very clean but you have to be careful with the water and take really good care of it, it's scarce. I 100% recommend this place and I will be back soon. I loved it!!

review_text: I had heard so much about this tour, mostly great experiences. There are a few rougue tours trying to cpompete but I did not personally hear any bad things about them. One bit of advice is that if a tour is trying to sell you their experience on or near full moon then they will be the copy cat operators. However, I did meet one chap on my travels who did exactly that and he had amazing pictures of the moon. It depends what you want really. For me, we had a completely uninterupted of light pollution night. We took the 9pm option as this was the english version. They alternate the 7pm and 9pm pickups for Spanish and English. The write ups to make sure you picked the company with the French owners and a Canadian guide were generally rated the best. The Canadian guide was on holiday so we had the owner. I expected and was told small groups and they had 10 telescopes. I also was informed that there was an observatory. There is not an observatory but there are 10 large telescopes. The group size was 28...that is not small at all. When we arrived it was very cold so really ensure you wrap up and some more. We stood around in the dark for the first 15 minutes while we were asked if we wanted tea, coffee or hot chocolate at the end. She kept asking for people to put their hands up, which you could't see so she could count. Why this couldn't be done on the bus en-route I don't know. Then we stood for the next 75 minutes listening to the main man talk and talk and talk and talk. 50% was astronomy the rest were sexest and obscure remarks and stories. HE was funny but it was not topical. We had 20 minutes to look through the telescopes. It was very disappointing for something that was potentially a once in a life time exciting option. One good thing is that if you have your camera it can be set up to take some amazing pictures so not all was a waste of time. It cost 18,000 Chilean pesos and their price is fixed. Other tours will discount for cash.

review_text: I took a tour that left from San Pedro De Atacama at 4PM and lasted till just after sunset around 8PM. The desert here is beautiful, and is almost completely void of plants. Our first stop was to visit some caves that we had to crawl through on hands and knees. That was interesting. We then saw the 3 sisters, or 3 Marias, which were some individually standing, maybe 20-25 ft tall rock formations, but only 2 of them are left, which was a shame. After visiting Monument Valley in Utah, I was not so impressed with the size of the sisters. We walked up a long hill on some sand dunes, which was physically difficult, but lead to some great views overlooking the park. When the wind blows hard, it whips up the sand which can blast your skin painfully. Sunglasses are a necessary protection, due to the wind blowing the sand. Also be sure to bring plenty of water a hat, (hold onto it when the wind blows!) and sunblock! Bathrooms are only available at the visitor center at the park entrance.

review_text: Before setting out for Chile, I knew this for sure: I have loved Pablo Neruda's poetry since I was a teenager. So, I board a micro 612 in Valparaiso to La Sebastiana, its four quirky floors overlooking the scenic Oceana Pacifico. Like a child in fairyland, I took in the ambience of poetic magic: the gilded figures and historic panels near the entrance, the famous wooden horse amidst the chaise lounges in his sitting room, the green goblets on a dining table set for one of his lauded dinners ~ and a door that made me laugh out loud. Marked Pedicure, it marked the restroom off the pink bar where Neruda tended to his guests' drinks. As a writer myself, I could barely tear myself away from his study, decorated with maps, Delft pottery and book-lined shelves. By evening, I was in love with Neruda and his Chile all over again. Sans doubt.

review_text: We had a wonderful experience with MTO and having, Carlos as our driver. On Wednesday night, my husband and I flew from Montevideo Uruguay to Santiago Chile. After we got our luggage, we easily found Carlos standing exactly where he said he would be, holding a big sign with our name on it. Carlos was very friendly and helpful and and the car was really nice, comfortable and spacious. He went above and beyond to assist us. On the way to the hotel he had Siri tell us what was going on in the city and then afterwards, he sent us links with restaurants and activities within the city of Santiago. He also was a huge help, helping me find my lost laptop at the airport. On Friday, after discovering my Apple laptop was missing, I fortunately was able to trace it to the airport terminal by using my “Find My Mac Air “ from my iPhone. I text Carlos and MTO tours , asking if they had any time on Saturday to take us to and from the airport in order to try to find my laptop. I got an immediate response, so we set up a time for Carlos to pick us up from the hotel and take us to airport. Not only did he give us a ride but he came in with us to translate and to navigate the airport. After talking with a few people , he led us down to the lost and found in the basement where we were able to retrieve my laptop! I don’t think we could have found it without him. He was as happy finding it as we were! I sincerely recommend using MTO tours for airport transportation. Taxis and Ubers can be challenging when arriving in unfamiliar airports, especially when one is weary from traveling. You also have to be very careful of illegitimate cabs that could be costly and possibly even dangerous. For comfort and safety , I recommend private transport, especially since the cost is not that much more. review_text: We had a great time with Gonzolo riding thru the foothills of the Andes on horseback. review_text: We attended the Patrimonial walking tour with SpicyChile and left halfway through, very disappointed. In our year long trip around South America we've been on dozens of walking tours and this was unfortunately one of the worst. The guide said his English wasn't great, and although it seemed OK to us we were let down by his lack of energy. On many walking tours guides help you learn about and fall in love with the city, but this tour was really tedious and boring. The guide spent more time making excuses for areas being trashed instead of giving us information about the areas visited. The sparce information he did give us was often incorrect (wrong names of churches, incorrect background on historical figures) as we took notes and researched the info ourselves. The final straw for us was when we stopped (about 45 minutes into the supposedly 3 hour tour) for a coffee break that we were told would last 15 minutes. Since we didn't want to order food from their handpicked cafe (kickbacks, anyone?) we had to wait in the park across the street for over an hour for the guide to finish his coffees. (At the hour mark the waiter put a new drink on the table.) Thankfully, while waiting we figured out that the tour info (the correct portion) is a copy of the Turistik.cl's bus tour info posted online and the actual walking route is the city's heritage walk which is posted on boards in the different plazas (Yungay, for example) with the route map and info in English. We finished the entire walking tour by ourselves hours before the group. Don't waste your time with SpicyChile walking tours, you can see everything on your own much faster and without the misinformation.

review_text: I hiked the O Trek and it was incredible! We were extremely lucky with the weather, only having some rainy or windy days. The views were picturesque and while the hiking was difficult, our guide Pepa knew when we needed to rest or slow our pace to ensure we didn't overdo it. The refugios (campsites) were well kept and almost all of them had all the amenities you could want (supplies for purchase, beer, and wifi if you needed). All staff members throughout the hike were kind and welcoming. Our guide Pepa was fantastic! She was knowledgeable about plants, history of the park and Chile, adventurers, and so much more. She ensured we were checked into each refugio on time, kept us up-to-date on expectations for the next day's hike/weather, and was a great companion to have on the journey. She and the porters that helped us (Coñeñe and Jaime) were kind and extremely helpful; they even brought us treats to have before each dinner which was a wonderful touch! Overall, the experience was unforgettable and Chile Nativo made it all seamless. I highly recommend the O Trek for adventure seekers, Chile Nativo as the organizers, and Patagonia for a memorable experience.

review_text: We rented a car from punta arenas, drove about 3 hours to puerto natales and stayed one night. We attended the 3 o'clock talk at Erratic rock which was very helpful info regarding logistics, weather, and gear. We got all of our gear and food that day then drove to the park the next morning. We booked our stay at konkashken lodge in Via Serrano, which is about 10 minutes drive from the Serrano park entrance (21,000 pesos for 3 day pass). Day 1 - we hiked Salto Grande to Mirador Cuernos, and did Mirador Ferrier. Day 2 - we took the Pudeto catamaran (30,000 pesos roundtrip) and hiked to Mirador Frances and back. The catamaran has limited times during shoulder season. In October, it left once at 11am and returned at 6:35pm. Day 3 - we camped one night at Torre Central and hiked to the base of the towers. This was our favorite hike as the visibility/weather were perfect. We enjoyed having a car and staying right outside the park, although the rental was quite expensive since we paid more for an automatic. We brought an extra tank of gas just in case but didn't end up needing it while we were in the park. We may have been lucky, but the weather was really nice! Bit cloudy at times, but would often clear throughout the day. Even though there was a fire that burned a large portion of the park previously, the mountains and lakes are really incredible. If we had more time, we would have wanted to complete the W or do the boat to grey glacier.

review_text: Do not take a tourbus if you are by car in San Pedro de Atacama. You have to be careful but the road from Atacama to El Tatio is not worse than a lot of other roads in Chili. We were on a big bus, maybe try to get a more private tour. When we arrived we saw a lot of small vans that arrrived earlier. Included in the tour was a visit to the village of Machuca. All inhabitants were gone and we were not surprised, it was really not interesting. Our guide was good enough, on request he stopped along the way at a big group of vicunas. But tours to El Tatio are simply not worth your money! The El Tatio geysers itself were not very spectaculair. Sure they were nice but it did not get spectaculair anywhere. But walk away from the group (if you get the time and are not pressed to have breakfast or go back to the bus for the next stop...) to see some nice pools and steams. If you can make your own tour you will enjoy the geysers more than we did. If you can't drive yourself there are more pleasant things to do around San Pedro de Atacama...

review_text: Fairly classic riverside market, well worth a visit. 3 things really interesting for me, beyond expectations. Gorgeous array of colourful fresh fish, fruits and vegetables, with lots of ceviche local made to buy on the spot, all in a covered but well vented space you can enjoy rain or shine. Watch and admire the fish mongers at work for a few minutes as they effortlessly clean and fillet the many fish on display with razor sharp knives. They make it look so easy and methodical, but if it was me, I would have sliced my fingers off in seconds! Plus, really cool that six or seven HUGE Sea Lions were just a metre behind them, (you could literally walk up and touch them!) taking the choicest trimmings while many more seals, sea gulls and vultures waited for their take further down the food chain. And it is all free to see!

Textiles, pots, metal goods, carvings, mummies all feature and there will be something here that you will amaze you, even if it's just the dates which show that these goods were being produced while much of Europe was inhabited by illiterate savages. It's not a huge place and an hour will give you time to see the masterpieces so, no excuses, get in there!

review_text: Apres a lovely light repast for lunch we used up our reserve energies in visiting a magnificent park which is elevated 300m above the city and features the imposing statue of the Virgin Mary at its peak. When i read that it also housed a botanical garden and a zoo, let alone biking & hiking opportunities, my desires were kindled. Without a doubt the summit is the highlight, from where the view is absolutely astounding, captivating and mesmerising. The Andes pokeup like jagged teeth, with slate-coloured clouds dashing across a peerlessly clear sky. The late afternoon produces a fusion of fiery orange colour with flaming pink, forcing everone near to sit, squat and pay reverence to this spectacle. Let me add, that a couple of sips from mote con huesillos, the trad dessert drink made from barley, stewed peaches and syrup, added to our contentment. Its amazing how friendly everyone is, while using the walking track, we pass and natter easily with locals as well as travellers like us. I attempt to use my silly-sounding Spanish with everyone practising their superb English

Our full day tour was about a 2.5 kayak in the morning, with a stop over for lunch on a beautiful farm overlooking Volcan Yates, and had another 1.5 hours of kayak afterwards. Winds picked up in one part but if you stay close to the coastline and listen to the guide, the waves are relatively easy. review_text: Together with my partner we took two tours with this agency, which we booked from Santiago. When we arrived at the agency, the people who assisted us from Expediciones San Pedro only cared about charging us the difference in the reservation, without offering us other tours or travel recommendations. On the first, the astronomical tour, they took us to the desert at night to observe stars. Upon arrival, the activity began with a 45-minute talk from the guide sitting on chairs outside, where between the harsh cold and the guide's story (which was hardly understandable), they gave us a very, very bad time. review_text: We did this tour (and all of our tours) with Cosmo Andino. And now that we've done it, I've got a few tips for a good experience. First, you absolutely need a great tour company with great vehicles and great drivers. (I highly recommend Cosmo Andino.) When they say that you are driving "off-road", it is not the American definition of off-roading. They don't mean a dirt or gravel road. They literally mean that there is no road. You just drive off into the open desert that has no tire tracks. You cannot do this on your own. Second, this is a HIGH altitude tour. We got up to 4800m (15,000ft)! I strongly recommend that you do a different high altitude tour before this to get acclimated. We were hurting on our first high altitude tour, but then we did much better on this one. I can't imagine what we would have felt like if this was our first high altitude tour. Third, the sun is serious here. (Did I mention the altitude?) I am a woman in my thirties with lots of thick hair, and my scalp got burned through my hair! (Like, my whole scalp, not just an area that was exposed by a part.) Everyone should wear a hat. Luckily, it's a bit chilly up there, so you'll probably be wearing pants and long-sleeves and won't need much sunscreen except on your face and hands. Fourth, bring binoculars if you have them. We saw lots of wildlife (vicunas, flamingos, llamas, birds) and it's great to see them up close. Fifth, drink water! It's really really helps to start hydrated. Once you get the headache, there's no getting rid of it until you come back down to lower altitudes. This was my second favorite tour. I know it can be pricey, but it's so worth it!

review_text: This place is stunning and there is no denying it however it is very busy with overflowing campsites and sometimes queues on trails. We did the W in December and this was only shoulder season. Book a camping spot if you are camping in advance to make sure you are not trying to pitch your tent into rocky ground in 70mph wind! We did not weigh our food so brought too much and this adds weight, definitely worth properly rationing, this was our error. The trails are busy and in places very poorly managed for the traffic they recieve. Considering the unchecked numbers coming into the park and the charge I would expect more. In addition you share the trail and campsites not always with people who have the same ideas about etiquette re rubbish, recycling and washing up... How ever as I already said the Torres are quite spectacular just be prepared to share it with many others. If wilderness is what you are after this is not it.

review_text: I took the glacier boat-trip in the first week of January 2010, which is mid-summer. The day trip begins at 0800 hrs from Puerto Natales, and we were going to experience the beauty of the landscapes of Ultima Esperanza Fjord. The boat left the port on time and we saw beautiful reflections of the city from the channel in the morning light. The temperature was rather chilly, so do bring layers of warm clothing, cap and definitely a wind-breaker jacket. We passed through Port Bories, which is an industrial cold-storage plant of historical interest. We saw lots of cormorants nesting on the cliff sides. We did not see the family of sea lions in their usual cave. It was probably due to the time of the year. I caught a beautiful rainbow on the Condores Cascade, which is supposed to bring good luck. Bridal veil waterfalls are everywhere at this time of the year. The Balmaceda glacier is receding rather rapidly, owing to climate change. The Serrano glacier meets the water of the lake (fjord) with intermittent calving, creating playful icebergs in the lake. One can take a half-hour hike to get closer to the Serrano glacier, or one can spend the extra hour taking fabulous photos. The forest is filled with all types of trees; specifically, the glacier is framed beautifully by cypress trees and other vegetation from the lookout point, just five minutes from the boat. After this, we took another two hours ride to the historical Estancia for a scrumptious meal of lamb and country vegetables. It took another forty-five minutes by boat back to Puerto Natales. It was 1800 hours, even though the scheduled arrival time was 1700 hours. The repast at the Estancia was quite the completion of a glorious day…….pisco sour, wine..

review_text: I joined yesterday the horseback riding tour of the Trancura agency in Pucon (one of the cheapest with 15.000CH$...later on I understood why!). I would like to propose to all future travellers to really pay attention to the agency they choose to book their activities cause even the simplest think like a two hour cabalgata could turn out bad... Unfortunately I had an accident (almost at the end of the tour) falling off the horse, which suddenly began to behave angry and run fast. Thankfully, I survived with only severe scratches on my hands and an injured swollen knee. I'm not an expert but I had riden before and am in good shape. My post is for reporting the bad conditions and the complete lack of organization of this tour. To begin with our guide in this horseback riding tour (we were 4 adults and a 10year old boy) was a 15years old boy...!!!! (It’s not possible for the agency to have control over all situations, they told as after the accident!) Furthermore the necessary equipment like helmets was totally absent and the guide didn't even carry with him a mobile phone to call in case of an emergency. And when this emergency showed up, the boy of course panicked and proposed to me to ride the horse again in order to reach the Termas which were really close. I won't mention the fact it wasn't so close, especially if you are injured, you can’t step your leg and feel dizzy from the fall, I'll just mention that I had to walk for some meters and then unable to carry on to wait for half an hour without knowing if a car will eventually come to pick me up for the hospital. I’m obviously not blaming the poor kid who works as a "guide" but the completely irresponsible agency that cooperates with equally irresponsible people, without even bothering to have experienced and qualified stuff. They nobody from the young guide to the people on Termas or the agency knew how to handle an emergency situation. And what if the fall was worse? When eventually a car came to pick up me and my friend who was with me, we had to drive first in the Termas Trancura, where they wrote down my data, and then wait for another half hour till they manage to communicate with the Trancura office in Pucon. The good thing is that the agency had insurance which covered the cost of the hospital in Pucon (more than two hours for an X-Ray on my leg, a doctor who didn’t checked me for concussion and a nurse to clean my hand injuries) but not the painkillers, the elastic bandage for my leg or the hospital in two days, when I have to go again to change the gauzes. I really believe that these issues should be managed legally and not just with a refund of your tour when complaining at the office or the answer "we're sorry but we can't control everything" just because they know their lack of security. An irresponsible agency like this one can be fatal. At the end of my post I would also like to mention the bad condition of the mules, which were tired or old, nervous and bad treated by the people of the farm. Good trips and be careful!

review_text: Vina Montes is very charming. Our tour guide Nastasia was the cherry on top! Ask for her. You won't regret it. Our tour started with a scenic ride to an overlook of the vineyard and drive by of the friendly llama pen. Montes uses goats and llamas to clean up the vines after the harvest. The wine production facility tour was fascinating, as was the view of the wine lab. However, the barrel aging room with the gregorian chants was almost unworldly. Between the smells and chants, it was really meditative. The quantity and quality of tastings was also superb. They also bring out the reserve good stuff! My favorites were the Montes Alpha M and the sparkling! Nas was quite instructive and illustratve with her knowledge and use of wine samples in her teaching. She even answered our wine vintage questions with vertical wine sample examples. I really learned a lot about their wine, chilean wine production, and the vineyard's history. Hoping they start shipping their sparking wine to the U.S. soon so I can order some to toast at my wedding!

review_text: This beautiful island is still a bit off the beaten track, though Chileans from the north have already discovered it and love its cool climate and lush green scenery (very much different from the hot and arid north). Probably the penguin colony on its west coast is seen as the island's biggest attraction, but I liked the beaches and hills bordering the Pacific ocean most. The birdlife is just astonishing and the picturesque villages are great for hiking to. Chiloé is easy to reach by public transport from Puerto Montt. The bus uses the frequent ferry across the Chacao channel and is convenient to reach Ancud (largest town) or Castro (regional capital). In summer the climate is pleasant and not as cold as Punta Arenas further south.

review_text: Decided on Summit Chile after researching several outfitters and could not have been more pleased with their level of professionalism and support throughout the hike. We arrived in Pucon on a Sunday and went directly to Summit Chile to get fitted. We had corresponded for about a month in advance to reserve the day and they provided helpful information and guidance about the hike and potential weather issues. When we arrived there was rain and snow in the forecast, so we were worried it would prohibit the climb the following day, but we ended up getting the green light and making the attempt. There were 4 guides for our group of 12 - led by Claudio who was fantastic. They were upfront with us that we had less than ideal conditions, and that we'd need to move at a faster pace to get to the top before bad weather set in. It was a pretty strenuous climb - made more challenging with the wind, snow and sulfur gas, which limited visibility at the top - but it was an amazing experience. We got to slide down for most of the descent, which was also very cool. This company had a great energy and spirit and we all enjoyed a beer when we got back. Would highly recommend.

review_text: We started out at Cachagua Beach viewing the island from the walk starting at the north-eastern end. However you really need binoculars to get a good look at the penguins. review_text: Two years ago we used LIz Caskey's services for tours in Chile. These were day wine tours out of Santiago and were excellent. This fall we would be in Buenos Aires and because of our experience with Liz's company in Chile we contacted her office about a day tour of the city. The itinerary was a morning tour of the city led by a guide with a car and driver. She took us to key locations of the city and provided comprehensive background on every location as well as points in between. We would leave our car and driver at each location, tour the area, and join up with the car to proceed to the next place. Our guide's local knowledge was very evident when we visited La Boca as this could be a difficult place to navigate. She also helped us with getting the right quality and price on some souvenirs. Her knowledge of the history of Buenos Aires and the political scene was outstanding. The second part of the tour was a private lunch with at a vinoteca with a sommelier who also owns a wine shop. This was very informative and we had a great lunch with wine pairings. After that leisurely lunch we joined up with her car and driver and went to the recently restored Teatro Colon. And following this we were taken to our hotel. A full day. My usual practice is to get a guide book and figure things out myself when touring foreign cities. Liz Caskey's organization put together an excellent tour and enabled us to experience this amazing city in a safe and secure way. Her tours are priced at a premium, but there is real value throughout.

review_text: On so many top lists of "things to do before you die" this park will truly make you feel like you have left earth and landed on a more beautiful planet. The most popular trekking route here is the "W" is not for total beginners. Its tough in parts and you need to commit to doing the course for 5 days if you want to do the whole thing. The weather down there is very unpredictable and you can go through all seasons in one day. Also, you will need to stay in refugios, rustic cabins, in bunk beds (8 per room) with potentially stinky and noisy room-mates, not much heat, and luke-warm showers. Basically, if you are from the US and don't have any camping experience, this would be "roughing it out." On the plus side you meet people from all around the world (we met Aussies, English, German, French, and a group of 12 elderly Polish people who were doing a "reunion" trek." Lastly, make sure you are equipped well. take a good sized water-proof backpack, water proof pants and hiking boots. More water-proof stuff you have better it is.

review_text: I’m surprised by the lack of reviews for this hike. This is a great, short, easy hike that gives stunning views over Lago Pehoe and Cuernos/Paine Grande Massifs. There is a small parking lot by Camping Pehoe right by the trailhead. It can be seen from the road. Be sure to tightly secure your belongings to your person before starting the trek. I’ll get to why in a minute. The trail leads through a forest of dead trees that were killed by the fire that ravaged the park in 2011. The trees, however, are hauntingly beautiful and they add to the beauty and enjoyment of the hike. Views are not obscured and you have a view of the mountains and the lake for almost the whole hike. Right before reaching the top you will come to a pass that is basically a wind tunnel. Again, be sure everything is secured. Unless you’ve lived through a hurricane, you can’t imagine the strength of the wind. It knocked me down twice, once into rocks and once into a prickly bush. It nearly knocked my 260 lb. husband down. Hold onto your hat because even if it is a beanie without a brim or bill, it can be blown off your head. This part is very short but you must get through it and round the corner to the left and you will be sheltered again until you get to the top. At the top, it is once again unbelievably windy. You could lean your whole body into the wind and you would not fall down. But oh the views are amazing! 360 views! It’s best to sit down and try to protect yourself from the wind as best you can. Try to snap some pictures just keep a good hold of your camera, make sure it is attached to you somehow. You probably won’t want to stay up there long but the view is incredible. On the way down, kind of on the left side of the hill, you can get a similar view that is sheltered from the wind. Then you’ll have to go through the wind tunnel again. It takes about 45 minutes to go up depending on how fast you are on how many times you stop for pictures. There is some elevation gain but It’s not very steep. It’s an easy hike just be prepared for the wind. We loved the hike, I highly recommend it. I think the winds are less in the morning but you may also get lucky with a less windy day.

review_text: Portillo is near the Argentine border, high in the mountains. The ski resort is situated on a beautiful turquoise lake named Laguna del Inca. My husband and I hired a guide to take us to Portillo for a day trip out of Santiago in March of 2002. It was off season, so there was no snow except for some in the tops of the distant peaks, but we wanted to see the Andes. The resort is up there all by itself. It is not a town, just a cluster of buildings. We ate an excellent lunch at the lodge and watched a short film about the resort. The lunch was expensive by Chilean standards. To get there you have to go up these turns called switches. I can’t remember exactly how many there are but each is numbered in the curve. I’ll guess around 20 turns. It was very slow going and a little nerve wracking when we would pass buses and trucks coming down. Along the way we saw goats on the mountain side and some wildflowers. title: Portillo, A Day Trip into the Andes from Santiago

review_text: if you're contemplating a visit to this park and considering whether the "W" or the "O" route suits you best, you will not go wrong either way. the shorter "W" has most of the highlights, and can be accomplished in 3 - 4 days quite comfortably. the "O" route incorporates all of the highlights of the "W", but as it circumnavigates the entire TDP massif, you will also get to enjoy the magnificent stretch between Campamento Seron and Rifugio Dickson, also the equally magnificent approach to Paso John Gardner east, and then the spectacular descent west of the pass as you journey to Rifugio Grey. you will no doubt also enjoy the view of the lake and the Glaciar Los Perros above it, just before you arrive at Campamento Los Perros. keep your eye out for "the finger of God" to the north about 90 minutes or so before you arrive at Rifugio Dickson (it is jutting dramatically out of the Southern Patagonia Icefield). the first half of that portion of the "O" route between Rifugio Las Torres and Seron (about 2 hours) is an uninspiring tramp through a nondescript forest, but otherwise (weather permitting) all other stretches of the "O" trail near-consistently offer either at least some nice scenery or the usual TDP stop-you-in-your tracks kind. many areas are quite exposed, especially along Lago Paine and over Paso John Gardner. we were rather fortunate overall with the weather, but these areas are notorious. perhaps it goes without saying that the rest of the route (the "W" portion) is also extremely enjoyable. we comfortably did the entire "O" route in six and a half days, the only back-breaker day was the 30 kilometer trek from Rifugio Las Torres all the way through to Rifugio Dickson. Faster trekkers can certainly shave a day or two off the total journey if they really keep moving, but you will have to either carry a bunch of gear with you (if camping much of the way) or plan on renting things at the various stops. Trail running is strictly forbidden apparently (though we did see a video being shown some place along the way of some Chilean trail runners who apparently did the whole route in 15 hours or something like that). the "W" portion can probably be done with a larger day pack as long as you stay at the rifugios and don't camp (and also don't stay at Rifugio El Chileno as the temperature can certainly drop at night, even at that modestly higher elevation); so you might be able to get away with simply a bivy sack on the "W" (though no matter what you'd better carry cold weather clothes with you as the temperature can easily reach less than 0 Celsius even in the summer, and can change rapidly). on the "O" route you'll be certainly be carrying a larger pack. why do the "O" instead of simply the "W" beyond the obvious additional scenic benefits? when we did our trip in late January - early February, the "W" portion was quite crowded; on the (northern) "O" portion we could commonly go a couple of hours at a time and see nobody else. you will probably not have much solitude any place on the "W" circuit - the difference was stark. this trail is not for the faint of heart - strictly speaking it's not very difficult in the conventional sense (there are not numerous steep or exposed sections, and only a couple of high suspension bridges, on chance of dehydration given the abundant water along the way), but those who are expecting the degree of trail maintenance found in most US or European national parks will be in for a surprise - heavy mud, swamp-like stretches, extended portions that feel like one's climbing a slippery, root-riddled ladder made out of mud abound. for those reasons alone, progress on some stretches will turn out to be nowhere near as fast as one might expect. on a general note about the rifugios - it's definitely essential to book in advance, especially for Rifugio Dickson and Campamento Los Perros (but probably for any rifugio, actually given how popular this park is becoming). the guardaparques (rangers) will inspect your papers at the Coiron ranger station and turn you back if you don't have proof you've booked ahead. also, there is a fairly big difference in quality between the quality of the two sets of rifugios you encounter - those run by "Fantastico Sur" are generally not as nice as those run by "Vertice", but you're kinda stuck as you can't plausibly stay at those run by the latter instead of the former. this is because along the way each site gets essentially a monopoly. not a big deal, but the vertigo-inducing confines of the Los Cuernos rifugio were abetted the afternoon/evening we spent there by the heavy rain outside (you may have to exhale completely to walk between the bunk beads here…). all in all, if nothing else such experiences will give you something to grumble about at the time, and laugh about later. one final note - the best TDP guide we could find to bring with us was Cicerone's version by Rudolf Abraham. unfortunately it is bereft of much of the useful information about logistics within the park (basically, you'll either have to thumb a ride along a very dusty road, arrange times with the Puerto Natales bus services to ferry you between spots if you need to, or arrange for a private transfer with one of the nearby hotels - the latter are expensive). Abraham's book is also shockingly non-descriptive of the scenery encountered along the various portions of the route, making it a bit difficult to weigh your options. we have relied on other Cicerone books on multiple occasions and they have been excellent - Abraham needs to take it to another level in my opinion, so you might shop around for something else.

review_text: If you have one day in Pichilemu it´s definitely worth a little detour past the punta de lobos surf spot to the Barrancas salt winning area. We didn´t do an entire ´ruta´, we just went straight to this place. But the road from Pichilemu to this place is alreay very nice. From Punta de Lobos it´s a 15 minute ride (10km) down the i500 and i520. It´s a bit further inland than the typical Cahuil village. Just follow the river until you have to make turn to the left (still following the road). At the end of this curve you can find this place, which is also a birds´reserve. We were there once in November and in August which is a big difference, because if the higher tides and the different salt winning process. I recommend to go in November/ December because there´s more to see. In August there´s not much to see because everything is underwater, in November all water was out and you can see much more of the process. Also there are some wooden bridges that lead you over the planes towards the bird reserve, but in August they are also underwater. The owner of the place is also the one who sells you the salt. They also have created a little exhibition explaining the process. Don´t forget to buy some salt, 5 kilos cost us like 3U$. If you go around lunchtime, we recommend to eat in Restaurant Marisol in Cahuil....they have amazing seafood for very reasonable prices!

review_text: So, this week we were in San Pedro de Atacama. We had a rental car (great way to explore the desert with as much time as you want!) and wanted to see the sunrise at Valle de la Luna to avoid the crowds. We got up in time, drove to the entrance at Mirador Piedra de Coyote...and then it was closed. We tried a second entrance of B241, but it was closed as well. Since we knew that Valle de la luna is a sacred place to the indigenous people there, we didn't want to invade it and just walk around the gate. So we ended up sitting on a dune just next to the entrance. While we still had a nice view of the sunrise, it wasn't what we got up for. On the last day in San Pedro we met a very nice guide and told him of our misery with the sunrise. He said, that usually in the small gate houses (that looked very closed to us) always two rangers stay the night and that we just should have knocked on the door and asked to be let in for the sunrise. Well, would have been nice to know that before. So if you go and if you are trying to see the sunrise at Valle de la luna, be sure to knock on the gate house!

review_text: We took the hikingtrip to Volcan Villarica with this company. We paid 150.000 pesos for two persons. Unfortunately, we were not really satistied. To start with a compliment, the company went out of their way to pick us up and drop us of at our appartment out of the town of Pucon. Our guide was a nice guy and a great hiker, but lacked some skills as a guide. Especially for people who are a little slower in the group, he doesn't give the feeling that it is a true team effort. We had bad weather all day, but went up all the way anyway. At the top the wind was extremely strong and it felt quit unsafe. Once back down, we'd noticed other groups had turned around. Seeing that the weather was this bad (no views once at the top), we felt the guide had better decided to turn around. There wasn't a lot of explaining about the area or the vulcano by the guide and neither about some of the equipment. We were for example told to bring the gasmask up to the top of the climb, but once there with the damps were pretty strong, there was no talk of how to use it. The way down was fun, sliding on the ice and our guide was very in his element, then even becoming a lot more attentive, himself sliding down the slopes on his shoes (!), but the feeling overall stayed the same: not really caring enough for the group, just going very fast. Because the hike and the ice sliding descend is so strenuous (a lot thougher than the website makes it out to be) this amount of care was a lacking. All in all we, pretty OK multiday-hikers, would recommend people doing the vulcano to pick another company, as there are loads. Or Sierra Nevada needs to improve their guiding.

Seeing that the weather was this bad (no views once at the top), we felt the guide had better decided to turn around. There wasn't a lot of explaining about the area or the vulcano by the guide and neither about some of the equipment. We were for example told to bring the gasmask up to the top of the climb, but once there with the damps were pretty strong, there was no talk of how to use it. The way down was fun, sliding on the ice and our guide was very in his element, then even becoming a lot more attentive, himself sliding down the slopes on his shoes (!), but the feeling overall stayed the same: not really caring enough for the group, just going very fast. Because the hike and the ice sliding descend is so strenuous (a lot thougher than the website makes it out to be) this amount of care was a lacking. All in all we, pretty OK multiday-hikers, would recommend people doing the vulcano to pick another company, as there are loads. Or Sierra Nevada needs to improve their guiding.

review_text: This stands at 4,300m high and is a stunning sight. The steam is better seen before the sun comes up so it's worth getting up extra early. And now the practicalities! (a) It was -5 when we went but no wind so didn't feel that cold. We wore thin merino thermals, a fleece, walking trousers and a thin Paclite waterproof jacket, woolly hat, gloves, thick socks and trainers. We bought this stuff for Patagonia and it doesn't take up much room. We couldn't be bothered to bring a huge thick coat to lug around for 3 weeks so layered up and were fine. Take a swimsuit if you want a dip in the hot pool (b) both gents and ladies loos have 4 cubicles so if there is a long queue for the ladies - just join the men! (c) drink lots of coca tea in the days before you go, you'll get used to it and it does help, and take some paracetamol or similar in case of a headache. All the guides are trained to deal with altitude sickness so go and enjoy the experience.

The views through the scopes were amazing esp seeing something that wasn't in our galaxy. We had plenty of time to look at everything and ask questions. Then we went inside for hot drinks and further questions. On the ride back you can get out nearer to your accommodation if it is en route. Wrap up warmly and take a torch for going home time. I really enjoyed this tour

review_text: It's a shame to have to write this because we really enjoyed the tours we got to go on, the guides were passionate and knowledgeable and the food provided was far better than we expected. Unfortunately though, the administrative side of Alabalti Atacama is seriously lacking when it comes to customer services and support. Our astronomical tour got cancelled about 10 minutes in due to cloud cover, which apparently couldn't be anticipated despite rain earlier in the day and the presence of constant clouds. Plus the tour wasn't actually run by Alabalti in the end but by another company which meant we couldn't directly speak with anyone that evening (the office closed before the start of the tour). We were told to contact our tour company for a refund or to rearrange the tour, but because we were leaving the next morning I sent messages that very same night to the numbers I had available explaining what happened and it took several days and several follow up messages before I got a response. Even when I did get a response, it was more important for us to be questioned about why we didn't go into the actual office for a refund than them trying to come up with a solution. We were informed that they couldn't refund the card we had paid with and they refused to incur costs from sending money to an international bank account. It's now reached a point where they won't even respond to our messages despite our trying to be patient and understanding. It's hard to believe that they completely lack contingency plans for when things go wrong, and as a result we've now lost out on close to £60 and who knows how long trying to find a resolution. For context the tour was supposed to take place on 7th March and it is now 26th April. We sincerely apologize for the frustration and inconvenience you have experienced regarding your refund. At Alabalti Atacama, we strive to provide excellent service, and it is clear that in this case, we did not meet your expectations. We truly appreciate your patience and regret that the administrative process has taken longer than it should have. We understand your disappointment regarding the Astronomical Tour cancellation, and we acknowledge that the communication and resolution should have been handled more efficiently. While weather conditions in Atacama can change rapidly, we recognize that there should have been a better contingency plan in place to address such situations. Regarding the refund, we regret the difficulties in processing the payment internationally. However, this is not an excuse for the lack of follow-up or responsiveness on our part. We take your feedback seriously and are reviewing our procedures to ensure a smoother and more transparent resolution process for future cases. We would like to resolve this matter as soon as possible. Please reach out to us again via contacto@alabaltiatacama.cl, and we will prioritize this issue immediately. Your trust is important to us, and we do not want this experience to define your impression of Alabalti Atacama. Once again, we sincerely apologize for this situation and truly appreciate your feedback, as it helps us improve our service. Best regards, Alabalti Atacama Team

review_text: We did a 4 day private tour from San Pedro Atacama to Uyuni and back with English guide. Both our guide, Oscar, and driver, Chino, went out of their way to make this a truly memorable holiday for us. The agency had the daily itinerary mapped out but Oscar and Chino worked on the fly to make sure we could stop whenever we wanted and spend more time when we met wildlife while still meeting the scheduling. Along the way, we came across numerous flamingoes, llamas, vicunas, donkeys, foxes, hares, viscachas and a rhea. The lagoons are a true sight and you would think that 3 days of lagoons is excessive but each lagoon looks different and the coloration of the mountains in the background is spectacular. Some points to note: as mentioned in other reviews, the last day of any tour which starts and ends back in atacama will be spent largely traveling. Private tours cost a premium but the hotel selection was great as was the level of service. Border crossing was also a breeze as we managed to skip the queues. Lastly, true English speaking guides are rare in Bolivia (ours had to specially be arranged from la paz) so book in advance if it matters to you.

review_text: This review is mostly about a tour agency Flamingo Tours. The Valley is quite a cool and unusual location, with bare a and cosmic landscape views. Worth a tour and hike while in San Pedro. The agency, Flamingo Tours, they need to get money signs out of their eyes. To the point: Terrible sales service, they just want your money. But they got some good guides who care. We came into the agency because it seemed respectable and the guy who was selling seemed friendly and interested in giving us an enjoyable service. Well, we were wrong. They misinformed us about the tour and lied to us about the payment, charging us more. The seller misinformed us about the tour, (which actually was quite good by chance, thankfully to great work of our guide Margarita and the driver, both of them saved our experience) because the guy who sold us the tickets only told us to bring warm clothes for Valle de Luna. The tour, however, involves some medium/hard hiking in the Atacama heat... And we were completely unprepared with clothes and shoes, and with small children... All because they did not provide full information when they sold the tour. Simply told us some names of the places included, without any real or useful information about the tour. Very disapponting, seems they just wanted to fill up the remaining spots in the vehicle and convince us to buy, rather than think about how to create a good experinece We were also diappointed by their lie regarding money, as they charged for two small kids and assured us that this was "normal" and "annoying" in Atacama and that at the entrance to the Valley we would also be charged for little kids at an adults price. A COMPLETE LIE. No one charged kids AT ALL and other agencies do not charge for little children either. Their office is hip and cool, and they have at least one guide who is passionate and really knowledgeable about the desert, its formation and history. But Flamingo as a company has to start listening and caring about the customers, or else we can find many other companies who really only want our money... In a place like Atacama it's a real shame to behave like this. The charm of San Pedro and the desert is in the people and in their genuine love for the place, as well as sharing it with travelers. That was what we came here for, and if you take the seller and his boss out of the equation, it was just that breathtaking and great experience in the desert.

review_text: The hill lives inside the Metropolitan Park in Santiago and it has a lot of exercise options. There's the road, which you can walk or ride to the top. There is also a lot of trail options for trekking or biking. I walked to the top via the road and a small trail. Via the road, there are a few stops to check the view and pickup your breath. There are also a few bathrooms and water spots along the way and some stops for picnics. When you get to the top, there's the catholic chapel which is amazing. There's also the Immaculate Conception statue and you can check the view from its sanctuary. If you want to grab a bite there are a few options on the top and if you want to try something local, you should try the Mote con huesillos or some empanadas. I went down through the main trail and it was quicker than the climb. Possibly my most favorite attraction in Santiago.

review_text: This monument honors the Chilean naval war heroes that that lost their lives in the 1879 Battle of Iquique during the War of the Pacific with Peru. At the top is Frigate Captain Arturo Prat, surrounded by Lieutenant Serrano, Sergeant Aldea, midshipman Riquelme and an unknown sailor. Four naval battles with the dates they took place are depicted in relief on the base of the monument. Underground a vault contains the remains of Prat and other offices who participate in these battles. What a wonderful tribute and remembrance to these brave sailors. Plaza Sotomayor and the monument are a must-see to honor Chile’s Naval history.

review_text: As noted, a very early start (4:30 am) but quite a spectacular display. It was very cold (15 below!) so make sure lots of layers. The geysers are only visible in the very early morning and have a ghostly, black and white presence because of the time and the massive clouds. Close-ups are very interesting to see the bubbling, spewing water. If great interest were some small pools of what looked like greasy water but which apparently are of great interest to NASA because those pools apparently hold the oldest living matter and scientists study these pools in relationship to possible life on other planets! pretty amazing. By noonish, it all just looked like a big, flat pasture. Worth a visit!

review_text: Today we took the glacier tour with Patagonia Planet and they picked us up at our hotel in PN. They were late picking us up (0630) and an hour and a half late yesterday but that is not the inconsiderate part. We picked this tour for the reason it was a half day. They pick you up, take you to the boat and take you back to the city. Simple enough. Well after the glacier tour we all went back to the van to leave. The drive told the entire van we had to stay at the hotel because one couple wanted to eat lunch at the hotel restaurant. WHAT?? He said there was nothing he could do because he is only a driver and didn’t work for Patagonia Planet. Nice enough guy but these two people caused the entire van full of people to sit in the lobby while they ordered drinks and lunch. One person in the van actually said something to the couple with no avail. After several people from the group talked to the driver he even went into the restaurant to say something but they actually ordered more drinks. We didn’t get back to our hotel until around 1700. It’s not good business to let one person change the schedule for an entire van full of people. Would not recommend. review_text: My husband and I traveled to Santiago, Chile for a work related meeting. Since we had traveled all the way to Chile from the Midwest we decided to extend our trip and spend several extra days in Patagonia. We flew flew from Santiago to PUQ and were meet at the airport by our guide, Kris Chamorro, and driver,? (So sorry we can’t remember his name). We headed to Punta Arenas and checked in to our very nice (but nothing fancy) hotel. We spent the day walking around the town and had dinner at our hotel with our guide. In the morning we got in our car and headed to Torres del Paines National Park. We enjoyed a pleasant 5ish hour drive to the park. Along the way Kris gave us some historical information as well as information about the local birds and animals. We checked in to the Hotel Las Torres upon arrival. The room, again, was very nice. All meals were included, they consisted of buffet meals with something for everyone. Our second day was a wondereful, amazing challenging hike to the base Torres (at least that is what I think it is called) ! We have done a lot of hiking in Colorado and when I say this is one of the hardest, but amazing, hikes I have ever doneI am not kidding. It was worth every bit of the 10+ hours and ?? Miles we hiked. The next day we took a boat to Glacier Grey. This again was fantastic! We were almost close enough to touch the glacier! In addition, we had “beverages” with glacier ice in them. Our last day was spent touring around the park to see the beautiful waterfalls and other scenery. We were driven to the airport for our flight back to Santiago, Kris waited until we were checked in and safely through security. I can’t say enough good things about our “team” they were wonderful. Kris has never met a stranger. And she did an excellent job of reading us to determine what amount of privacy vs interaction we wanted. If you are traveling to this region i would highly recommend planing an adventure with this company using the guides we had. One thing to be sure of, if you are traveling in a group we would suggest that you check to make sure everyone in the group is at the same level of fitness. The tours (hikes)must cater to the lowest level of fitness. No one will be left alone at any time on the hikes. Dear Norma, Many thanks for your feedback. We are very pleased to hear that you enjoyed your days in South Patagonia with us. We will be happy to show you other parts of our country if you are coming back in the future! Best wishes, Teresa Montes & BirdsChile team

review_text: Travel by rented car in Calama. It was not a 4x4. We left at 4:15 from San Pedro. Along the way we stopped a couple of times to appreciate the stars. We had Google directions for the route, but they were not necessary because everything is well signposted. The condition of the road is good, dirt but compacted, until Guatín. From there the road presents quite deep cracks in sectors. More or less at km 55, almost upon reaching the Vado Putana, a fairly long area of calamine begins (more or less 12 km) that in some parts is of an extreme level that becomes endless. The agency minibuses passed us at full speed through that area, but a city vehicle could suffer serious damage to the cushioning if one travels at the same speed. After about 1 hour and 45 minutes of travel, the visit to the geysers is of course worth it. The return trip can be done more slowly to appreciate the landscape of the area. There are vicuñas in many areas, as well as flamingos and vizcachas in the fords (Putana and Machuca) and, if you are lucky, some condors in the heights. The town of Machuca offers breakfast for visitors, as well as llama anticuchos, goat cheese empanadas, among other things. The picturesque church can be visited from the outside. Further down, there are cacti in the ravines. I didn't give the experience 5 stars because of the state of the road. In my opinion, there is no reason why they can't pave this route, especially given the large number of tourists who come to see the geysers.

review_text: The ascensor is actually called Ascensor La Concepción, commemorating the heroic battle (from which no Chilean soldier survived, massively outnumbered as they were) that took place in Perú while it was being built in the early 1880s, not just the cerro itself. This is worth knowing, as this period of expansion was the high point of Chilean self-confidence and of Valparaíso as a port. Ascensor La Concepción links the main commercial street (with its various names all commemorating the same War of the Pacific) with a residential zone inhabited at the time by, among others, the English, German and Dalmatian communities, which is evident in street names, churches and long-decomissioned school buildings. The views from within the ascensor are only partial, but it has an atmosphere all of its own.

review_text: We did a 3 day private Tour with our amazing guide Eddy from the Chilean Border to the Salar de Uyuni. You notice right away that they have done theese tours for a long time because it was super well organized. We had a spacious 4w4 car and started at the bolovian side of the border, saw unbeliebably beautiful landscapes and took hundreds of spectacular photos. It really is one of the most beautiful landscapes we have ever seen, and we have travelled a lot before! The first day is spent in a very remote region, you can see Geysirs and lots of Wildlife (Vicuñas, Flamingos). The hotel of the first night is located at 4500m, in europe you would only expect a basic hut in the mountains but here we were served a 3 course dinner! I did get altidude sickness which resolved the next day when we descended do 3500 m. Some reviews stated that the hotel (Tayka del desierto) gets really could but that was definitely not the case at our stay, we felt cozy and warm during the night! The highlight was the Salar the Uyuni where Eddy took absolutely spectacular fotos of us. We saw them covered in Water which produced an otherworldly giant mirror effect. When we booked our flights we were unsure wether it would be a good idea to see the Salar in the rainy season, but to br honest we think it looks even better covered in Water (We saw dry salt flats in argentina for comparison). This was definitely one of the most special Places we ever saw, the memories of how beautiful Bolivia can be will stay with us! review_text: I came to Santiago earlier this week with a group of my peers, and we decided to take LBV's afternoon tour. However, the tour was much more detailed and comprehensive than our original prognosis. Our tour guide Jose Miguel stopped us every 10 to 15 minutes to tell us all about the history of the country of Chile, explained the significance of local landmarks, and really taught us so many things about the country and the city that we could not have learned in a text book. I cannot recommend this tour enough, as my whole group had a blast, and the three hours passed by extremely quickly. They even have a few surprises for you, but I'll let you figure those out on your own.

Magellan himself stands at the top of the monument gazing out to sea. It really is quite a spectacular work of art and both the monument and the surrounding plaza turned out to be the highlight in Punta Arenas.

review_text: I chose Cruz Andina for their reviews and they did not disappoint. Regardless which company you choose, it all stands and falls with the guide. Gilmar (Patcho) has made our trip a very memorable one, he greeted us with a bright smile and already after 100m in the car he acted like we were stuck in a riverbed, but then started laughing and we moved on. We knew we were in for a great ride. He was a fantastic photographer, suggested funny group pictures along the way, explained about flora and fauna and cared for us throughout. Pricing: the companies vary slightly, but expect to pay about 150.000 CLP + 300 Bolivianos in cash for the trip (entry to the park, hot shower, snacks, note: all the tour companies indicate these additional costs in advance, so people complaining in reviews about extra costs just did not listen) Also: tip the guide at the end, don’t be cheap about it, compared to them, we are all very priviliged, even if you are a student ;) Know what to expect: this is a trip into very remote areas of Bolivia, so don’t expect a 4 star treatment, but long hours on bumpy roads, basic food and basic lodging in exchange for jaw dropping nature and a trip of a lifetime. Guides usually speak Spanish only. Don’t forget: Water (3l each, you can buy more along the way), toilet paper, immodium (trust me) ;) Have a fun trip!

review_text: This private museum is unique as its permanent collection is mainly about Latin American artists and some European artists.The goal of its founders, Harry and Martine Recanati, was to bring Latin American artists into the public eye with Ralli Museums in Uruguay, Spain, Israel and Chile. We were here about 3 years ago and were delighted to see that the paintings and smaller sculptures had changed. We were told that the collection regularly gets changed with the other 3 museums which makes it a museum you can come back to over and over again. This museum with its 2 floors is very well laid out and the works are beautifully placed especially the very big sculptures that by the way never get changed because of their sheer weight. Artists are among the top that Latin America produces or has produced among whom Roberto Matta and Mario Toral of Chile, Wilfredo Lam of Cuba just to name a few. I was the most impressed though with the sculptures made Mario Aguirre, Mexican artist. His sculptures and the likes fill the halls and make a statement that Latin America does count in the art world. What a little treasure! Don't miss it when in Santiago! And it is free! Muchas gracias por tus comentarios y recomendar a Museo Ralli Santiago para los que visitan la ciudad de Santiago. Saludos cordiales, Museo Ralli Santiago

review_text: Rustic campgrounds. Smelly bunk rooms and smellier bathrooms. Rain and wind. Toe blisters. Why would anyone want to do this? Because the O Circuit is simply one of the best treks in the world. Antares Patagonia and especially their sales manager Fernando did a great job of setting up our trip and answering our many questions. We were a group of four plus our guide Anna. She speaks English, German, and Spanish and is extremely knowledgeable of geology, flora, fauna, and history. Anna went above and beyond the call of duty; like Mary Poppins she pulled unexpected items out of her backpack (which weighed fully half as much as she does) — a French press coffee maker, fresh avocados, a bottle of hot sauce, a veritable pharmacy of medical supplies, and a bottle of wine. Anna always had a smile on her face, even when cajoling us to step up for the tough but spectacular hike over John Gardiner pass. I know we paid a princely sum for our trek but the added bonuses and reduced stresses realized by going with this fine company was well worth it. Anna could not conjure up a sighting of a Magellenic woodpecker but she did find us a pair of rare Torrent ducks diving and feeding in turbid white water. If you have the stamina and time, do the O and not just the W. There are spectacular features like the Grey glacier that you won’t see on the W and it is MUCH less crowded because CONAF only allows 100 people a day to start the O.

review_text: had the most incredible experience on this guided tour from Santiago, visiting the breathtaking Inca Lagoon, the charming InSitu Vineyard, and an adorable little llama sanctuary. Definitely something you don’t expect to enjoy as much as you do! What made the trip even more special was our guide, Seba. He was incredibly knowledgeable and passionate about the history, geography, and culture of Chile. He kept us all engaged with fascinating stories and facts throughout the day. And shoutout to Oscar, our driver, who navigated the mountain roads smoothly and safely, and was also a pro with the camera – capturing some amazing shots of the group and the scenery. If you’re looking for a memorable day trip from Santiago that combines nature, culture, wine, and adorable animals – this is the one!
