review_text: I just returned from doing the 4 night/5 day W trek in Torres del Paine National Park- booked through Fantastico Sur- and wanted to share my experience To provide context, I've done a lot of hiking and treks including Mount Kilimanjaro so I don't discount what I say thinking I may be an inexperienced hiker. Professional Trail Guides: You absolutely do NOT need a professional guide for navigational purposes on this trek. The trails are unmistakably marked, you are given a trail map when you enter the park and there are plenty of other people walking the exact same route as you. Hiring a guide for the purpose of navigating the trails is totally unnecessary. Operators: I looked into booking the refugios directly versus with an operator and found that it was most economical to book a "program" covering all refugios and meals with Fantastico Sur. Fantastico Sur owns most of the refugios anyway and have priced them to encourage you to book a program versus booking a la carte accommodations and meals. The reality is that there really aren't any options in the park anyway because FS owns almost everything. Even if you camp you are doing so at Fantastico Sur operated camp sites. Getting To The Park: Fantastico Sur provides bus transportation from Puerto Natales (PN) to the park and some logistical information for getting to PN from Punto Arenas. They were not at all helpful to me in finding information for getting to PN from El Calafate (EC)- where I was staying before/after the trek (they literally ignored my email inquiries). On my own I discovered there are two bus companies going from EC to PN (companies: Zaahj and Cootra), each with one departure daily from EC to PN (oddly, more departure options were available in the reverse direction). Both companies have websites but do not facilitate booking tickets online. Tickets must be purchased in person at the El Calafate bus station. We arrived EC in the late afternoon needing a bus ticket for the next day. Cootra was sold out, Zaahj had availability. When we arrived the following morning to depart NEITHER bus operator's office was open- meaning had we needed to buy a ticket that morning we could not have purchased one from either bus company. The bus cost ARS$140 and took 5 hours going down and 7 hours coming back. At the Chilean border you must go through customs (takes 30 minutes to 1+ hour). We arrived PN and went directly to the FS office where we received our bus ticket for transfer to the park, another couple hours drive away (actually a bit of backtracking). Annoyingly, FS told us in advance that their bus from PN to the park departed at 230pm but when we arrived they told us the bus was leaving at 2pm. Luckily we were there in time but we easily could have missed the bus. The FS bus is a miserable experience, no A/C, dirty bathrooms and unreliable rest stops (one bus driver refused to let us off for a break at the gas station). On our return day it was terribly hot outside and because there are neither open windows on the bus nor A/C people were literally overheating en route from the park. It was an absolutely dangerously hot situation on the bus... totally irresponsible of Fantastico Sur to load people into what was effectively a greenhouse without air circulation or venting. BRING WATER, snacks and toilet paper for the bus! Arrive early to get front seats. Refugios: We stayed one night in each of three refugios and one night in the lodge on the west end. Camping at the refugios was a cheaper option (with our without carrying your own gear) and in hindsight we are VERY glad we did not do this. Fantastico Sur will sell you an option to camp without having to set up your own tent but even that option is incredibly unappealing, having now seen what the campgrounds offer. The campgrounds are adjacent or near by the refugios but their bathrooms are DISGUSTING. At the time we passed through the refugios campers were telling us of a single toilet being provided to the ENTIRE campground, no running water or toilet paper or showers etc. Additionally, slower hikers arrived to find that no camp sites remained due to over booking and as a result they were forced to set up tents next door to the sewage facilities! I did not meet a single camper who was pleased with his/her experience, every single one of them wished they had stayed in the refugios. The refugios themselves are nothing but hostels (6-8 people per room) but they do have formal bathrooms with multiple toilets, running hot and cold water and 3 story bunk beds. Unfortunately at Refugio Cuernos we encountered bed bugs which stayed with one person in our group through the remainder of her trek until she was able to get out of the park and wash everything in her possession. The bed bugs made for a MISERABLE experience for our friend. (Note: once back in EC we learned from other people that bed bugs in the refugios are VERY common) Unfortunately, because Fantastico Sur owns most of the refugios and the camping situation is unbearable there really isn't an option as to where to stay in the park. At Cuernos there are cabanas (adjacent to and more expensive than the refugios) which might be a little safer with regards to bed bugs than the refugios because less people stay in them. The cabanas also have a single shared hot tub which is not available to refugio guests or campers. Meals: Meals at the refugios are edible, but nothing to be excited about. You must fill your water bottles from the bathroom sinks. Very little water is actually served with the meals. We had fish with mushroom sauce the first night, a huge cut of pork and mashed potatoes the second night, shepherd's pie the third night and pasta with tomato sauce the last night at the lodge. A vegetarian option is available which amounted to little more than a can of palm hearts and a can of fava beans. Breakfast each morning was the best meal of the day: scrambled eggs, toast with jam, instant coffee and tea. Lunch each day is a huge sandwich (tuna one day, palm hearts with mushrooms one day, tomato and cheese one day), an apple or an orange, a bag of trail mix, a granola bar and a chocolate bar. Money/Purchases: The only items available to buy in the refugios are cookies, crackers, candy bars and wine. I believe they accept both Chilean pesos and USD. Weather: We arrived with plenty of cold weather and wind gear but encountered an unusual hot spell so all we needed were socks, shorts and t-shirts. The trails are very exposed to the elements so whatever weather is out there you will feel it all (wind, rain, snow or sun etc). I met people all along our trip who experienced every kind of weather possible so it's really impossible to know what to pack. I would say the most important pieces of gear include a hat, rain coat, sunscreen sturdy hiking shoes (it's very rocky and you hike a lot of miles each day) and flip flops for the refugios. Trails: No matter what anyone else says remember this: the W is NOT an "easy" hike! Hiking to the Torres themselves is ALL uphill. Hiking from Cuernos to the end of the French Valley to the lodge is a 17 mile day! I definitely think the W is worth doing- and definitely recommend going all the way to the end of the French Valley rather than stopping at the Italian camp- but do not underestimate how much strength/stamina is required. We saw plenty of people who tuckered out and heard stories of others crying alongside the trails due to exhaustion. One group we encountered rented their car and spent two nights at the east end in the Torres refugio for a day hike up to the Torres then two nights in the lodge on the west end for a day hike to the French Valley and back then another day hike up to the glacier and back. I'm not sure if their mileage was more or less than hiking the W through from end to end but they certainly had the advantage of staying at the *nicest* places and avoiding Refugio Cuernos. To be fair, Cuernos is in a beautiful setting but it had the worst food, visible bed bugs, overflowing campgrounds and a horrific and pervasive sewage odor. Summary: Puerto Natales has nothing redeemable- get in and out as quickly as possible. If you're coming from El Calafate buy your round trip bus ticket to/from PN the moment you arrive into EC. Fantastico Sur is a miserable operation but you don't really have any choice other than to use them in the park. If you elect to camp and carry your own gear or cook your own meals be prepared for a back breaking experience carrying all of that extra weight. I would never recommend camping on this trek and in hindsight I would have booked the cabanas at Refugio Cuernos in an attempt to avoid the bed bugs.

review_text: This is the first review I have ever written on Trip Advisor... I stumbled upon The Uncorked Cooking Workshop almost by accident. But I must say, I am glad I did. I know I will never be a chef. I will never remember every detail about all the wines I have tried. I probably won't even remember the names of all of them either. However, our experience with Connie & Jose Miguel's cooking workshop reminded us that those things are not what matter most; what matters is the experience you have. Connie is an excellent teacher and her passions for food and family are contagious. She was so easy to relate to (and spoke excellent English). The setting was in a large, "rustic" kitchen. All of which made you feel like you were making dinner at a good friend's house. It did not feel like a class or a restaurant at all. In addition, the recipes were simple and yet bursting with flavor. Connie picked the dishes based on our preferences and she was spot on. I couldn't have asked for a better meal or better company. You don't have to dice an onion perfectly or prepare everything "by the book". Recipes can change based on your preferences and do not have to be complicated. I loved the Uncorked Cooking Workshop because it reminded me that the experiences are most important. I would recommend it to anyone who loves to eat and enjoy good company.
title: Traveling is about the people you meet and the experiences you have.

review_text: We booked the 5 day self trekking hike called the "W" (the classic route) with Ecotours, making it easy for us having all bookings at Refugioes, for transport etc. arranged by them, but still hiking on our own. Super service all along from booking to briefing at the start. Torres de Paine is beautiful, we enjoyed every day walking through very different nature, topography and every day having different views. We hike a lot in Norway and we have done a lot of hiking in many countries but this is absolutely one of our favorites. If you are an experienced hiker the hike is relatively easy (about 20 km per day), (but we also met many people that "had taken on too much"), but it is so varied and with so many stunning views that not a single moment was tiring. Having everything arranged by EcoTours was superb. It was a very nice arranged set-up, everything worked out perfectly well. We arrived at the airport in Punta Arenas, got the bus to Puerto Natales (we had booked hotel ourselves) and started hiking the next morning after a short briefing in their offices where we got all the vouchers and tickets for bus, meals, accommodation, boat etc, Many people do the "W" in 4 days and to our opinion, they miss one of the highlights! On our 4th day we stayed at Refugio Grey (a small nice refugio, small and charming), and got there relatively early to leave our backpacks. Then we continued a couple of hours across the second suspension bridge to see close up the Patagonian Ice Field. Absolutely worth it, it was amazing. Most people go to the first look out and return to Paine Grande to catch the boat the same day. They miss out on the best part! The short briefing we received in Puerto Natales the night before the trek was excellent, some of the things that were highlighted turned out to be excellent advice. Be sure to have good shoes, warm clothing, and rain gear. Other than that, you can buy “everything” in the refugios if you need food, beverages, some types of equipment etc. The only negative experience (which is not anything Ecotours can influence) was the welcome to the national park. It was designed to scare of people who potentially would cause a fire (with big forest fires behind, it is understandable that they warn unexperienced hikers, but there is no need to threaten with the “30 years in Chilean prison”. It turned out as a real propaganda). In addition all the buses into the park let their engines go while waiting- not very environmentally friendly and also very noisy. That having said, overall, it was a very good experience; we would definitely love to come back and e.g do the circuit. And NB important to add: the staff at the refugees was, with no exception, really friendly and helpful. We were impressed by the effectivity with serving so many, it really worked well. At the same time it never felt really crowded. Hi Gunn, thanks for your great review and for tips on Torres del Paine extra Hike! Looking forward to welcome you in Chile soon! Best, Cristian

review_text: Santa Lucia is a piece of Chilean history and a wonderful place to view part of the city. is highly recommended. An interesting climb with steep steps and wonderful vegetation in parts. Sometimes the sprinklers are on and your climb has a just sprinkled, refreshing quality to it. We were there on a very hot day and this was an excellent feature. It is a small hill but the views from the top are worth while. It is also nice to see the fountain and the statues at the entrance. Fort Hidalgo is at the top of the hill. Built to defend the hill Fort Hidalgo was finished in 1820 as a defensive point. On the other side of the hill was a cemetery for dissidents, non-Roman Catholics. In 1872 president Bejamin Vicuna Mackenna decided to remodel the hill by building a road, a chapel and a park with fountains and lookouts. Fort Hidalgo is now a place for events to be held: weddings, birthdays and other special occasions. I certainly wish I could attend one there.

review_text: I am backpacker, 37yrs old, 40+countries visited. I visited Mamalluca observatory encouraged by good reviews on Internet. That was my second observatory, my first experience was in San Pedro de Atacama. PRICE: 4.500 pesos for the entry, 3000 for return transport with a mini van arranged in a ticketing office in Vicuña (the lady in the ticketing office also reserves the transport). WEATHER TIP: The observation of the stars depends strictly on the weather conditions, so before you make a reservation check weather forecast. Vicuna has normally clear sky in most of the days but you never know. We arrived to Vicuña on a cloudy day and we were told in a ticketing office that it's better to wait a few days so we went to Pisco de Elqui instead for two days. When we returned to Vicuna we were advised to buy a ticket at 8pm for the tour at 8.30pm if the sky is clear, which we did so. TRANSPORT: I did not have any problems with the transport from Vicuna, minivans were punctual (by the way ticketing office was still open at that time) taking us from ticketing office (15 min drive) and taking you back straight after the tour to the center of Vicuña. You are back by 11.30pm. PROGRAM: ** 9pm start of the tour, English/ Spanish groups to choose ** observation of Mars, Saturn, stars with the telescope inside the observatory with a dome roof and adjusted watching space and guide explanations ** observation of Milky Way, clusters with a telescope outside ** presentation in the observatory building: digital display of pictures of stars and planets and the moon, explanation of astronomy website 'stellarium'. ** finish about 11pm ***** there was no observation of the moon. IMPRESSION: - Too many people, lack of silence, there were 3 groups for about 15-20 people each including young Germans talking and laughing constantly - the guide should learn how to execute silence especially from people who do not appreciate opportunity; - observation outside was at the same time for all groups which means that you hear other guides in the background and you can see other laser pointers in the sky... - Guide's commentary was not structured well which was a shame cause he was very knowledgeable. It was more questions - answers type of a tour but he spoke very good English. - Mars and Saturn was very small and the image was blured, we did not observe the moon and there was no option to choose the tour with the moon observation - I had some questions to the guide at the end of the tour but I was rushed by a driver to finish which was not very nice. OVERALL: I expected very good standard after reading reviews but after my experience in San Pedro de Atacama I found it disappointing, overrated with way too many tourists for a tour. For my partner it was the first observatory and he said he would not have visited it at all. I visited a private small observatory in San Pedro (10.30pm-12.30am) with just 5 people in total, we observed the planets and stars (the telescope view was much better then but I think it might depend on the timing) and then waited for the moon which was the most impressive. I liked digital presentation though, very interesting.

review_text: I found Carlos and Extremo Chile online and they seemed like the best option for visiting Chilean Patagonia in the Winter. I am part of a group of exchange students from the US studying in Santiago so we only had a few days to visit the park and we were restricted in that we couldn't rent a car. Because of this, we organized a custom 6 person program through Carlos that was three days in the park with two nights in small cabins called refugios close to the hikes. For about $450 per person, Carlos included our buses between Punta Arenas and Puerto Natales, a van and driver for the three days in the park, all park entrance fees, the lodging, and all food for the time in the park cooked by our awesome guide Francisco Parada. Francisco also has his own business for longer backpacking trips. I'm sure we could have done it all for much cheaper during the summer when camping is more feasible but we basically had the whole park to ourselves, whereas a lot of the popular sights are full of people during the high season of summer. If you are in Santiago for the winter or want to visit the park in the off-season I highly reccomend Carlos and Extremo Chile! Carlos: extremochile@gmail.com Francisco: INFO@OFFTRAILPATAGONIA.CL

review_text: This is a review for the winery tour experience. The residences were damaged by the earthquake at the time. At $40 per person for the tour, one would expect an amazing tour and tasting. For what it is, the price is obscene and offensive. Sure, the wine is quite good, but the tour experience is pretending to be high class and feeding off its "best wine of 2005" status, when in fact, it is quite mediocre. Upon arrival, we were told we were late (only 5 minutes) and then we were served corked wine (you know what it smells and tastes like - horrible) and the guide suggested that perhaps we were wrong. She didn't even taste the wine! That said, the building itself, built in 2005, is quite beautiful - the 24 wooden "ribs" around the outside of the building represent the months the wine stays in the barrel as well as a bird's nest. The ttasting room/barrel cave resembles the inside of a barrel and is very impressive. Still, not worth the $40 if you've been to other winery tours before. But. if you only have time to visit a couple of wineries in the Colchagua Valley and $$ is not an issue, then go for it. Just don't expect the service you should get for such a high priced tour.

review_text: Being a middle aged European couple you are not that brave anymore, but would like to still feel " young and active", so when I found Jass on Trip Advisor, I felt she was the one. More trekking in the national park and learning survival skills and again enjoying fantastic views. Both Jass and Juan Pablo are two very professional, very knowledgable people and what they don't know about nature to church construction isn't worth knowing. We felt safe and comfortable all the time. So glad we did it, and would not hesitate to do it again. Review of: Kayaking at Poza

review_text: When people travel to Chile, they always visit Santiago, Valparaíso, Viña del Mar and a couple of wineries. Although these are very nice tours, they are losing a must go in the country: the infinitely charming and adventurous little town of Pucón. There, you can raft, you can mountain bike, ride quadricicles, horses and just shop, get to know mapuche culture, and eat at cosy delicious charming restaurants. Or you can do its greates adventures: climbing Volcan Villarica. It is one of the most active volcanoes in the world. The ascension is exhausting, but the view of the crater and the immense landscape is totally worth it. Butt-sliding down the volcano is infinite fun. I recommend choosing a well reviewed tour agency for hiking Villarica (which is actually mandatory according to national regulations).

review_text: My wife and I just completed a trip to Patagonia last week and it really was the trip of a lifetime due to Venture Experiences. We started planning this trip about 18 months ago and Carrie was absolutely fantastic with providing options and adjusting the itinerary to meet our needs and interests. Creating, coordinating and scheduling an itinerary with multiple lodgings, a variety of activities and transportation between each location is certainly doable on your own, but not easy. We looked for someone that was “local” and has access to connections that we probably would not have found. We are very, very glad that we leveraged the expertise and local knowledge of Venture Experiences. I have to admit that it was not an inexpensive trip, but it was also SO MUCH MORE than what we anticipated. We really didn’t have a specific purpose for going to Patagonia, like doing the entire W-trek, but we did want a flavor of what Patagonia is and was. Our personalized Venture Experiences itinerary hit the mark in every aspect. Valentina, our guide for the two weeks, met us at the airport and immediately set the tone for exceptional customer service. We only hiked about half the W-trek, including surviving the climb to Torres del Paine (we jokingly refer to this as the Towers of Pain”). The two-day hike from Centro over to Paine Grande was “easy” in comparison. We’re not “spring chickens” anymore, and we did actively prepare for this trip knowing that we’d be doing a bunch of fairly difficult hikes. Our preparation was barely adequate, yet it helped immensely that Valentina evaluated our abilities, broke things down daily and encouraged us every step of the way. The National Park is stunning and you have to be there and experience it in person to really appreciate the raw beauty of Patagonia. Pictures do not do it justice. We had to make adjustments to our plans mid-trip due to weather and Venture Patagonia was right on top of things. The capstone of our trip was the stay at a remote cabin at La Estancia where we spent 3 days riding backcountry on horseback with spectacular views of the fjord and Mirador glacier. This portion of the trip would never have happened if we hadn’t enlisted the aid of Venture experiences to arrange our itinerary. We cannot say enough good things about Venture Patagonia and their attention to detail and service. We highly recommend them to anyone contemplating a personalized trip to Patagonia.

review_text: This place is great for all sort of activities. Conveniently located in Santiago's city centre, you can have a great time visiting the zoo, enjoying the views from the finicular, having a picnic, go swimming (Tupahue swimming pool open only during summer)... and everything in the same place! If you're the sporty type, going up to the top of the hill either cycling, jogging or just walking, is a very enjoyable activity, especially in autumn or spring when the temperature is mild. At the top of the hill you'll be able to access The Virgin Mary's gigantic sculpture, sanctuary and chapel. An open air space with great views of the city. You'll also be able to get any sort of refreshments, icecream and 'mote con huesillos", a cold an sweet beverage very popular among Chileans made of dried peaches boiled in sweet water and wheat. Loads of calories in it but something your body will thank you for if you opted for cycling to the top! The access to San Cristóbal hill is free, but obviously you need to pay to enter the zoo, the funicular, teleférico or the swimming pool. If you're not the walking/explorer type, you could take the teleferico to the hill top from Pedro de Valdivia Norte access and then take the funicular down to the Pio Nono access, which will lead you to the always busy Barrio Bellavista, where you could finish your day having a fab meal in one of the hundreds of restaurants you can find in the area. This is a very turistic area, but the quality of the food in the restaurants that offer sort of 'fusion food' is exceptional!

review_text: Liz planned a private tour for us in Chile and Argentina in late February 2013. She took care of every detail including hotels, tastings, restaurants, transportation and everything was beyond perfect ( including the weather). We emailed back and forth to finalize the trip but she quickly was able to put together a trip which met our needs including giving us time to explore on our own as well as guided tours. She was upfront on what was included and the costs and gave us a detailed schedule so we knew exactly what was involved. We arrived at noon in Santiago and were whisked to our lovely hotel with a fabulous courtyard including a waterfall and, most important, our first pisco sour (and then our second). The next day it was off to the markets with Liz herself and then back to her apartment for lunch. A great introduction to the culture of Chile - and the food and wine and the gelato. The rest of the trip gave us a variety of experiences focused on wine and food but with lots of other things as well in both Chile and Mendoza Argentina - we went biking, toured heritage sites, visited a school for kids at risk and a dairy. Everything was really fascinating from the winery where they produce both olives and wine to the cooking class we took learning to cook for the mud oven. And finally the Atacama Desert which we had never heard of and visited at Liz's suggestion - it turned out to be a highlight of many highlights - viewing the stars, biking to salt ponds, and then floating in the salt water, vistas of the Andes, the salt range, flamingos. Beyond incredible. We could have stopped the car every five minutes to take pictures. We totally enjoyed everything on this trip and all the folks who were part of the trip - Liz, the guides and drivers and the folks at the wineries other spots we visited and the hotels. They were all super knowledgeable and great to talk to and learn from. Liz was totally on top of all the details and made sure everything went smoothly. We are still enjoying the memories in our very busy lives and for sure we are going to be back and will use Liz to plan our next trip to South America.

review_text: We tried to book this tour, which is free, but couldn’t because it was booked out. We tried to book 3 months ago. The wait list was also booked out. We went to the bus depot, which is where the buses leave from, on the Saturday morning, at 8.30, hoping to get 2 places allocated to us from ‘no-shows’. No chance. It didn’t matter how much he protested, he was turned away. So, if you do secure tickets, get there with half an hour to spare. At 8.45 on the dot, if you are not there, your seat will be reallocated to a hopeful, if there are some waiting. We didn’t try on Sunday as a lot of the Hopefuls said they would try again the next day. ALMA only run the tours on Saturday and Sunday. The road turn-off to ALMA is on the main road south east out of town heading to Toconao and Socaire but has a security gate, as you would expect, and you cannot get in without a pass. We tried unsuccessfully.

review_text: My friend and I were unsure of our plans in Copiapo and when we decided to go to Pan de Azucar, we took a risk of planning it ourselves. It ended up being a fantastic experience so I want to give my advice to future visitors (keeping in mind we went in mid-June, during the off-season): Rent a car from Europcar (~$80 for 24 hours) and drive up route 5 from Copiapo to Pan de Azucar. It is a very easy and smooth drive so don't worry about the road conditions. The last part of the drive is on a dirt road to the park but it is completely safe and relatively smooth. Once at the park, (5000 entrance fee), drive to Mirador trail and hike that (2.5 km) if you are looking for a shorter experience (other trails 10 km +). It was a beautiful ~2 hour hike through desert with sand, cacti and mountains for as far as the eye can see. If you’re lucky (which we were), you might even see some wild animals like alpacas! This trail ends at a gorgeous viewpoint overlooking coast/beach/ocean/cliffs. In general, Park is very hard to access/see well without a car so renting a car is the easiest way and is relatively cheap too. We also drove to Bahia Inglesa on our way back which is off of route 5, 30 km from copiapo, between copiapo and pan de azucar. This was a beautiful beach with restaurants and nice sunset. Both are a must see in the Copiapo region!

review_text: After (too?) much food and wine in Santiago, we were happy to spend the day hiking with our guide,Alejandro, and an entertaining group of fellow travelers in the Cajon de Maipo. We were promptly picked up at our hotel and shuttled to San Jose de Maipo where our guide and driver arranged boxed lunches. Be sure to bring at least 2 liters of water for the dusty hike that follows! The terrain was not overly taxing, but ascended for 6 km amidst the beauty of an active volcanic area. Our hike was characterized by gorgeous coloured layers of sedimentary and volcanic rock comprising the peaks surrounding the valley at the end of which loomed the El Morado glacier. We hiked for several hours past free range horses and mineral springs until we lunched at the lagoon at the foot of the glaciers. After our return to the van, we bounced our way to the Banos Colina, an almost natural set of pools at the foot of San Jose volcano. Alejandro outdid himself in local knowledge, fascinating conversation, and attention to detail that included wine and snacks after a revitalizing soak. First class! We are happy you enjoyed your day with us! Thank you or the review :) Marine D. community manager at Ecochile

review_text: My wife and I booked this trip many months ago in the hope of seeing a puma, which had been one of my main reasons for coming to Torres Del Paine. Our guides Carlos and Kevin (with his skilful driving and tracking) were absolutely marvellous! We departed in a comfortable 4WD vehicle in pre-dawn darkness with a drive to the eastern side of the park. After a relatively short time Kevin got tip on an area where a puma might be and then he spotted a puma ( named Petaca) moving parallel with the road. I could not believe we would see her so close and she seemed quite unbothered by us and others. I was able to get some good photos. Later in the morning we watched her from a distance again. Carlos prepared hot coffee for us for a break by the road with a nice outlook, then we went searching again. We had lunch at a great spot near the Welcome centre for Torres del Paine ( the sun was out and the clouds parted to allow great views of the towers). Then we set out again. This time we find Petaca elsewhere and just sitting by the side of the road resting in shade. Later Kevin spotted another one (Dania) just west of Amarga centre in the hill - I don’t know how he can spot them so well! Again we were able to watch it come down from the hill and cross the road in front of us. The whole arrangements were very good and Carlos was a wealth of information which added nicely to Kevin’s driving and spotting skills. Kevin also took some great photos himself with his 3000mm zoom camera and he shared them with us a few days later. I highly recommend this company and the tour. It was well organised, informative and fulfilled one of my dreams for our visit to Torres Del Paine. Carlos and Kevin are great company! 🙌🏻🙌🏻

review_text: This museum is a really worthwhile experience for several reasons; first of all it is located in an extremely attractive colonial era administrative building, the "Palacio de la Real Aduana". Inside are really two separate museums. The upper floor houses a traditionally organised collection of pre-Columbian art from other parts of Latin America with including some beautiful masterpieces. These are arranged by geography (but not chronology which confusingly means you may jump a thousand years when going from one case to another). The collection is not big but there are some beautiful works, especially from Mexico (Olmec, Mayan) and Peru (Mocha) and Bolivia (Tiwanaku). However the real higlight is the basement which is a self contained and recently opened museum of artifacts from Chile. You descend deep down by dimly illuminated stone stairs as if back in time, to a large single underground space organised by cultures and regions (e.g. Rapa Nui, the Andes). There are interesting and informative descriptions and the objects themselves are beautifully lit and organised. Unlike the upper section, this part of the museum focuses as much on cultural history and context, as showing artistic objects (for example I enjoyed the cabinets exploring the significance of the Shamen in Andean culture and the role of Chicha). Both upper and lower museums are worth visiting, but if pressed for time the downstairs section should not be missed. There is also a very pleasant cafeteria which has good cakes.

review_text: I recently went to the astronomical tour offered by Astrotours while on my honeymoon and I cannot recommend it enough. It was an unforgettable and fantastic experience and definitely one of the best tours we took during our stay in San Pedro de Atacama. Astrotours offers transfers which will pick you up at the hotel you're staying and will take you directly to their site. The site itself is located just outside San Pedro de Atacama and it's only a 15/20 minute drive from the city center. The tour is guided by Patricio, an extremely knowledgeable and kind astronomer. He is very didactic and the entire experience is also very educational as he is very eager to answer any questions you may have. Usually, each tour is made in groups of 10/15 people. It gets a bit chilly at night in the middle of the desert, but don't worry! Patricio and his team offer a generous amount of wine, liquor and other non-alcoholic beverages to keep you warm. Astrotours offers two telescopes for you to gaze upon our galaxy's celestial bodies and you can even have your own picture taken under the stars by Nathan! Our group consisted mainly of Spanish speakers, so the tour was entirely in Spanish. I believe they also offer tours in English, as we were asked beforehand if anyone present had any difficulties understanding the Spanish language. All in all, an unbelievable experience and highly recommended! Review of: Astronomical Tour with Guide and Pick Up San Pedro de Atacama

review_text: I did a 5-day self-guided W trek tour to Torres del Paine with Chiletour Patagonia in April this year. It was a very nice experience! The walk itself is superb but most importantly I think I've found a right tour company that gave me confidence to do the walk by myself. I found ChileTour Patagonia totally out of luck because there were not many tour companies still organised tours (even self-guided ones) to Torres del Paine in mid April, even if there were some, their prices are unreasonably high during low season. Ricci, the owner, quoted be good price and replied my emails quickly (I have to say this is very unusual for any tour companies in Southern America, they tend to respond really slowly, some don't even bother answering you especially if you don't understand a word of Spanish!) At first, I was a bit worried to do the trek by myself because I am not so much a trekker and my sense of direction is just T~E~R~R~I~B~L~E~ !!! but thanks to Ricci!!! he gave me very detailed guidelines and plans for my trip that put my heart at ease. Just few days before my trip, I got a message from Ricci that he was not able to brief me in person when I arrive as he had something urgent. He then arranged Flippe and Ricci's assistant to come and pick me up. I had a terrible night with owner at Wild Hostel from Puerto Natales who refused to keep my massive backpack as they promised before I headed off early next morning. It was 11pm by the time I arrived that hostel. I was soooo glad that Ricci had sent people over to my hostel and so they helped me to look after my backpack and store it at Ricci's place for the next 5 days while I was doing my walk! During my stay at the Park, I once again felt so lucky that I had Ricci to organise all my accommodations and meals. I met friends who did the walk without any agents, ended up they have to pay a great deal just for their accommodations. As for meals, if you are not with an agent, you have the options to buy your meals at different refugios but once again, that will cost a lot in the end. With the meals that Chiletour organised for me, they are massive and includes all the nutrients that you need for each day. Sorry ~ I've got many good stories to share with this company as I had experienced a looooot crazy ones while I was in South America! If you ask me if I will do tours again with Chiletour Patagonia, that's a DEFINITE YES! Thank you Xuly!

Some mention was made of pre-columnian tribes etc, nothing of the Spanish Colonial period, absolutely nothing until Allende in 1970. No dates given for any buildings, no architects - and all of this to a group of foreigners. When I asked what happened before Allende, I was told there was not time to discuss this - although almost all the buildings were waking beside, were built in this period! Sadly, this was a waste of my time. Hi Sandy N, Thank you for giving us feedback on your tour with us. We value every comment as it allows us to improve our services on a daily basis. I would like to apologize for not giving you the tour experience you expected. It has taken us more than 10 years to perfect our tours and we have made a conscious effort to focus our tours more on culture, local idiosyncrasies, politics and current issues rather than things one would find on the Wikipedia page about the city. That being said, every guide should be able to answer questions related to history and architecture when they arise. We’ll make sure it doesn’t happen again. Cheers, Peter

review_text: We did the tour to the Geysers. The pick-up was on time at our hotel. Our guide, Erik, was very friendly and had lots of knowledge on the places we visited. We drove straight to the Geysers (1.5 to 2 hours) where we got out of the van and visited the geyser field for about 45 minutes. Our driver prepared a breakfast with toast, eggs, cheese, coffee, cookies, etc. that we ate next to the geysers. Then we went to the hot springs (45 minutes there) and on to a native village (30 minutes), Machuca where we could buy llama meat and goat cheese empanadas. We also made several stops to look at the wildlife - vicuñas, birds, viscachas. Erik gave us plenty of time to visit all the sights and let us also explore on our own. The size of our tour was good, we had 14 people total which is the maximum for the Whipala tours. The price/quality ratio is really good and I recommend Whipala.
